# Min-Plus Convolution Lower Bounds via a Higher-Order BSG Theorem

Nick Fischer<sup>∗</sup>

Ce Jin<sup>†</sup>

Yinzhan Xu<sup>‡</sup>

**Abstract**

_Min-Plus Convolution_ is a central problem in fine-grained complexity, and the associated Min- Plus Convolution Hypothesis forms the basis for a wide range of conditional lower bounds for fundamental problems. It is closely connected to the APSP and 3SUM Hypotheses, and in fact implies both, making it a unifying hypothesis for two of the main pillars of the area. In this work we establish several strong results related to Min-Plus Convolution. We design a _universe reduction_, showing, under a plausible additive combinatorics assumption, that the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis is _equivalent_ to the _Strong_ Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis. We also obtain tight conditional lower bounds for multiple long-standing problems, including Min-Max Convolution and Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution.

Our approach is inspired by Fischer’s recent equivalence between several variants of APSP [S ’26], but extending that technique to the arithmetic setting requires overcoming deep obstacles. To this end, we develop a novel additive structure theorem that can be viewed as a higher-order substitute of the Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers (BSG) theorem, allowing us to extract strong additive structure even from weakly structured sets. Building on this structural result, we show that certain structured 3SUM instances (namely, sets with low _rank_) can be solved in truly subquadratic time. This algorithm forms the main algorithmic ingredient in our reductions. Besides, it generalizes _all_ previously known truly subquadratic-time special cases of 3SUM, and is therefore of independent interest.

## 1 Introduction

The _Min-Plus Convolution_ problem is one of the central problems in fine-grained complexity. Given two integer sequences _A_ and _B_ of length _n_, the task is to compute the sequence _A∗B_ where (_A∗B_)[_k_]=min_<sub>i</sub>(A_[_i_]+_B[k-i_]). Naively this takes time _O(n_<sup>2</sup>), and the fastest known algorithm achieves only mild improvements, \(n^2/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{logn})}\) \[Wil18\]. This leads to the _Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis_ \[CMWW19, KPS17\] postulating that truly subquadratic time \(O(n^{2-\epsilon})\), for some constant \(\epsilon>0\), is impossible.<sup>1</sup> This hypothesis has been used to establish conditional lower bounds for problems including Knapsack \[CMWW19, KPS17\], Unbounded Subset Sum and the Frobenius problem \[Kle22\], Integer Programming \[JR23\], Tree Sparsity \[BIS17\], hop-bounded shortest paths \[KP23, VXXZ25\], and an approximate version of 3SUM \[BGK24\].

Beyond its many applications, the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis plays a central conceptual role in the landscape of fine-grained complexity. It is closely connected to the famous _3SUM_ and _APSP_ Hypotheses, and in fact implies them both \[BCD<sup>+</sup>14, BIS17\]. Thus, it can be viewed as a unified hypothesis of two of the main pillars of the area. In particular, the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis is one of the strongest well-established hypotheses, implying more conditional lower bounds than most other fine-grained assumptions. This makes studying Min-Plus Convolution a fundamental problem in its own right.

In this work, we establish several strong results that significantly sharpen our understanding of Min-Plus Convolution. We design a _universe reduction_: assuming a plausible hypothesis from additive combinatorics, we show that the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis is equivalent to its _strong_ variant, which asserts hardness even for instances with integer weights bounded by _O(n_). As a consequence, we obtain tight conditional lower bounds for a variety of long-standing convolution problems with "intermediate" complexity, including Min-Max Convolution and Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution.

### 1.1 Starting Point

Our starting point is a recent breakthrough by Fischer \[Fis26\], which establishes analogous results for the APSP problem. Specifically, Fischer shows that the APSP Hypothesis and the Strong APSP Hypothesis are equivalent, assuming a plausible hypothesis from additive combinatorics and that \(\omega=2\). He further shows that the Directed Unweighted APSP Hypothesis, stating that APSP in unweighted directed graphs requires _n_<sup>2.5-_o_(1)</sup> time, is in this equivalence class. This greatly sharpens our understanding of the role of the universe size in APSP.

Given that Min-Plus Convolution and APSP are similar in many ways, one might wonder whether Fischer’s technique transfers. In particular, can it be applied to show the equivalence between the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis and the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis?

At a high level, Fischer \[Fis26\] follows a structure-versus-random approach that could, in principle, apply to any problem _P_, and that has already been successful in other fine-grained reductions \[ABKZ22, ABF23, JX23, CVX23\]. It can be summarized in three generic steps:

(1) Identify a suitable measure of _structure_ for _P_.<tbc>

(2) Show that _P_ can be solved fast on _structured_ instances.<tbc>

<sup>1</sup>Unless otherwise specified, the entry bounds of all problems we consider are polynomially bounded in the input size. The postulated lower bounds hold in the Word-RAM model with \(\Theta(logn)\)-bit words, and hold against potentially randomized algorithms.

(3) Then, suppose that we aim to design a fine-grained reduction from _P_ to some other problem _Q_. Given any instance of _P_, we first repeatedly extract structured subinstances, and solve these subinstances with the fast algorithm from step 2. Once there is no more structured subinstance, we regard the remaining instance as _pseudo-random_, and exploit the pseudo- randomness in the reduction to _Q_.

Of course, successfully implementing this approach hinges crucially on the choice of the structure notion. It has to be weak enough so that structured instances can be solved efficiently, but strong enough so that the corresponding pseudo-random instances can be exploited in the reduction.

In Fischer’s setup, _P_ is the APSP problem (or rather, for technical reasons, the equivalent _Min- Plus Product_ problem), and the relevant notion of structure is a matrix rank parameter known as _select-plus rank_<sup>2</sup>. A major technical contribution is a fast algorithm for instances of low rank, from which the universe reduction and further lower bounds follow via the general framework.

Let us return to Min-Plus Convolution. As the analogy to Min-Plus Product is strong, a priori one may hope that Fischer’s techniques can be extended to Min-Plus Convolution without too much difficulty. However, our situation is quite the exception. Obtaining the analogous results for Min-Plus Convolution poses several substantially new obstacles that are not present in the matrix world. First, it is entirely unclear what the appropriate notion of structure should be for sequences or sets. This naturally falls into the realm of additive combinatorics; however, any such notion must capture _extremely weak_ additive structure, far from the commonly used strong structure measures. This leads to a second major challenge: the existing tools from additive combinatorics are not well suited for this regime, and we need to invent our own structural results. All in all, our route involves three steps, each of which is interesting in its own right:

• We develop a new additive structure theorem that can be viewed as a "higher-order" substitute of the Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers theorem (Section 1.2).<tbc>

• We then identify the appropriate structure notion, called _rank_ in analogy to \[Fis26\], and show that low-rank instances of Min-Plus Convolution can be solved in subquadratic time, based on the new structure theorem. In fact, we directly work with the harder 3SUM problem (Section 1.3).<tbc>

• Equipped with this new algorithm, we derive the aforementioned universe reduction and strong lower bounds from Min-Plus Convolution in analogy to Fischer’s proof (Sections 1.4 and 1.5).

## 1.2 A New Additive Structure Theorem

Using additive combinatorics in fine-grained algorithm design and complexity is an exciting recent trend \[CL15, BW21, BN20, BN21, ABF23, JX23, CVX23, Jin24, Bri24, CLMZ24, BFN25, FJX25, AFJ<sup>+</sup>25, CMZ26, Fis26\]. This was pioneered by Chan and Lewenstein \[CL15\], who introduced the celebrated Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers (BSG) Theorem to our community, and derived various strong algorithmic consequences of it. The BSG Theorem has since found many more applications \[CL15, ABF23, JX23, CVX23, FJX25, AFJ<sup>+</sup>25\], notably also in Fischer’s work \[Fis26\], and became an important part of the fine-grained toolkit. To understand both the strengths and the limitations<tbc>

<sup>2</sup>The _select-plus rank_ of an \(n\times n\) integer matrix _A_ is the smallest number _r_ such that there exist matrices _U,V_ of sizes \(n\times r\) and \(r\times n\), respectively, so that \(A[i,j]\in\bigcup_{k=1}^r\{U[i,k]+V[k,j]\}\).

<tbc>of the BSG Theorem--and how we overcome them--let us take a short excursus into additive combinatorics.

Intuitively, the BSG theorem states that any set _A_ with a lot of "local structure", e.g., in the form of many solutions to the equation _a_<sub>1</sub>+_a_<sub>2</sub>=_a_<sub>3</sub>+_a_<sub>4</sub> for \(a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4\in A\), must admit a large subset _H_ that is "globally structured", in the sense that the _sumset_ \(H+H=\left\{a+b:a,b\in H\right\}\) is small. Such sets _H_ are also called _low-doubling_ sets since their _doubling_ \(\frac{|H+H|}{|H|}\) is small. To state the BSG Theorem quantitatively, let us introduce a piece of notation that will turn out convenient later:

\(\mathrm{Pop}^k(A;p)=\left\{x:|\{(a_1,\dots,a_k)\in A^k:x=a_1+\cdots+a_k\}|\ge p\right\},\)

i.e., the set of all sums \(a_1+\cdots+a_k\) that can be expressed in at least _p_ distinct ways. We refer to these as the _popular k-sums_. Then the BSG theorem can be equivalently stated in the following (non-standard) form:<sup>3</sup>

**Theorem 1.1** (BSG Theorem, Reformulated)**.** _Let_ \(A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _be a set with_ \(\mathrm{Pop}^4(A;|A|^3/K)\neq\emptyset\)_. Then there is a set_ \(H\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _satisfying that:_

• \(|H|\le|A|\) _(in fact, we can take H as a subset of A),_<tbc>

• \(|H+H|\le K^{O(1)}|H|\),<tbc>

• \(|A\cap H|\ge|A|/K^{O(1)}\).

In other words, the existence of a popular 4-sum certifies the presence of a large low-doubling subset.

Unfortunately, the BSG Theorem is insufficient to deal with sets exhibiting much weaker additive structure. Consider the following example. Let _A_ be a random size-_n_ set in a large universe {0_,...,u_}, say for _u=n_<sup>10</sup>. In this case, with good probability, each 4-sum is unique. In particular, there are no popular 4-sums. This is consistent with the fact that _A_ contains no large low-doubling subset. Nevertheless, _A_ is not entirely unstructured: it is contained in a much larger low-doubling set, namely the entire universe {0_,...,u_}. The challenge is that this weak global structure is invisible to the 4-sums. Our key insight is that such weak structure can be detected by moving to larger _k_-sums. Specifically, we show that for sufficiently large _k_, the presence of a popular _k_-sum reveals the desired structure. This leads to the following higher-order analogue of the BSG Theorem.

**Theorem 1.2** (Popular _k_-Sums Imply Low-Doubling Structure)**.** _For every c\>_0 _and_ \(\epsilon>0\)_, there is some_ \(k=k(c,\epsilon)\) _such that the following holds. Let_ \(A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _and assume that_ \(\mathrm{Pop}^k(A;p)\neq\emptyset\) _for some_ \(p=\Omega(|A|^{k-1-c})\)_. Then there exists a set_ \(H\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _and some_ \(K=O_{c,\epsilon}(|A|^\epsilon)\) _such that:_

• \(|H|\le K|A|^{1+c}\),<tbc>

• \(|H+H|\le K|H|\),<tbc>

• \(|A\cap H|\ge|A|/K\).

<sup>3</sup>To relate Theorem 1.1 to the usual BSG Theorem (e.g., Theorem 2.3), note that _A_ has a popular 4-sum, \(\mathrm{Pop}^4(A;|A|^3/K)\neq\emptyset\), if and only if _A_ has large _additive energy_, \(E(A)\ge|A|^3/K'\), where _K_ and \(K'\) depend polynomially on each other. The "if" direction is immediate by Cauchy-Schwarz. The "only if" direction follows from some basic Fourier analysis and Hölder’s inequality (see e.g., \[JX23, Lemma 2.11\]).

To illustrate how to apply the theorem, consider again the example from before. We apply Theorem 1.2 with _c_=9, and for some arbitrarily small constant \(\epsilon\). The theorem then chooses some constant \(k=k(c,\epsilon)\). There is indeed some _k_-sum in _A_ that is \(\Omega(|A|^{k-1-c})\)-popular (as there are |_A|<sup>k</sup>k_-sums taking at most _k|A_|<sup>10</sup> distinct values), satisfying the premise of the theorem. Theorem 1.2 then implies that a large part of _A_ is contained in some set _H_ of size at most _K|A_|<sup>10</sup> and doubling \(|H+H|\le K|H|\). Here, the doubling \(K=O_{c,\epsilon}(|A|^\epsilon)\) is controlled by the initial choice of \(\epsilon\). I.e., we can force _H_ to be arbitrarily well-structured (as long as _K_ is polynomially large), at the only cost of increasing the constant _k_. Theorem 1.2 turns out to be a surprisingly powerful tool that is likely to find more applications beyond our specific interest related to the Min-Plus Convolution problem.

The proof of Theorem 1.2 builds on the _asymmetric_ BSG Theorem of Tao and Vu \[TV06\], a significantly more intricate extension of BSG to pairs of sets of different sizes. In fact, our result is the first in fine-grained complexity, and even theoretical computer science as a whole, that exploits the asymmetric BSG Theorem, to our knowledge.

At a very high level, the proof of Theorem 1.2 is by increasing _k_ gradually and tracking the sets of popular \(\ell\)-sums for \(\ell=4,5,\dots,k\). By a pigeonhole argument, at some point, the popular \(\ell\)-sums and \((\ell+1)\)-sums correlate (both in size and structurally), at which point the asymmetric BSG theorem can be applied to extract the desired low-doubling set. We provide a detailed proof in Section 3. We also face the extra challenge that for our algorithmic applications, it does not suffice to know that _H_ exists, but we must be able to _compute H_. Therefore, along the way we also devise an efficient randomized algorithm to find _H_ as in Theorem 1.2 (see Theorem 3.5). Notably, to this end we also had to design an efficient algorithm for the asymmetric BSG Theorem (see Section 7). This black box will certainly be handy for other algorithms in the future.

Finally, let us remark that there are some other higher-order variants of BSG that have been studied in additive combinatorics \[SSV05, BC11, Shk14, Lee25\]. However, unfortunately none of these existing results applies in the weakly structured regime required for our applications (though some of the same ideas, e.g. as in \[BK11, Shk14\], turn out useful for the proof of Theorem 1.2 as well). This concludes our additive combinatorics excursus.

## 1.3 Low-Rank 3SUM

Equipped with Theorem 1.2 we are now in a position to start implementing the structure-versus- randomness approach following Fischer \[Fis26\]. Recall from before that the foundation of Fischer’s proof is to identify a certain _rank_ parameter, and to design a truly subcubic-time algorithm for computing the min-plus product of _low-rank_ matrices. An immediate challenge of extending Fischer’s proof to Min-Plus Convolution is the lack of such a rank notion. It is unclear what should be the rank of a sequence or a set with respect to normal convolutions, let alone Min-Plus Convolution.

A main contribution of our paper is to identify a suitable notion of rank for sequences, which is strong enough (so that unstructured instances are sufficiently pseudo-random to complete our reductions) but not overpowering (so we can still design a fast algorithm for Min-Plus Convolution on low-rank sequences).

In fact, we will directly work with _3SUM_, a harder problem than Min-Plus Convolution. Given three sets _A,B,C_, it asks to decide if there is a solution to _a+b=c_ for \(a\in A,b\in B,c\in C\). 3SUM can be solved naively in time _O(n_<sup>2</sup>), and the _3SUM Hypothesis_ speculates that it cannot be solved in truly subquadratic time. This hypothesis is among the "three big" fine-grained assumptions. As mentioned before, Min-Plus Convolution reduces tightly to 3SUM, and for this reason we prove a<tbc>

<tbc>stronger statement by showing that low-rank 3SUM is in subquadratic time. Another advantage is that the structure measure can be defined for sets rather than sequences, which turns out cleaner:

**Definition 1.3** (Rank)**.** The _rank_ of a set \(A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\), denoted _r(A_), is defined as the smallest integer \(r\ge 0\) such that there is a set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) of size _r_ satisfying \(A\subseteq X+X\).

This notion has been considered before in the additive combinatorics literature, see, e.g., \[EN77, BvHK25\].<sup>4</sup> Observe that the rank of _A_ ranges from \(\lceil\sqrt{|A|}\rceil\) to |_A_|+1. Sets with low rank are considered structured; for instance intervals or arithmetic progressions have rank close to \(\sqrt{|A|}\). At the other extreme, random-like sets have rank close to |_A_|. We show that for sets with rank up to \(|A|^{1-\epsilon}\), 3SUM can be solved in subquadratic time:

**Theorem 1.4** (Informal Theorem 4.1)**.** _Let_ \(\epsilon>0\)_. Any 3SUM instance_ (_A,B,C_) _where one of the sets has rank at most_ \(O(n^{1-\epsilon})\) _can be solved in time_ \(O(n^{2-\epsilon^\prime})\) _for some_ \(\epsilon'>0\).

Interestingly, Theorem 1.4 generalizes and unifies _all_ previously known special cases of 3SUM that are known to be in truly subquadratic time:

• _Small-Universe 3SUM:_ When \(A,B,C\subseteq[u]\), 3SUM can be solved in time \(\widetilde{O}(u)\) by the Fast Fourier Transform. This is truly subquadratic when \(u\le n^{2-\epsilon}\). In this case, all three sets have rank \(O(\sqrt{u})\le n^{1-\epsilon/2}\) (witnessed by \(X=\{0,1,\dots,\lceil\sqrt{u}|-1\}\cup\{\lceil\sqrt{u}|,2\lceil\sqrt{u}|,\dots,\lceil\sqrt{u}|^2\})\).<tbc>

• _Small-Doubling 3SUM:_ As a vast generalization to Small-Universe 3SUM, Abboud, Bringmann, and Fischer \[ABF23\] and Jin and Xu \[JX23\] considered 3SUM on inputs with \(|A+A|\le K|A|\), and gave truly subquadratic time algorithm provided \(K\le n^\delta\) where \(\delta>0\) is sufficiently small.<sup>5</sup> For example, \[JX23\]’s algorithm for this case runs in \(\widetilde{O}(Kn^{1.5})\) time, which is truly subquadratic provided \(K\le n^{0.5-\epsilon}\). As an improvement to their algorithms, our Theorem 1.4 implies a truly subquadratic 3SUM algorithm whenever \(K\le n^{1-\epsilon}\).

This implication follows from the following simple fact: if \(|A+A|\le|A|^{2-\delta}\), then there exists a set _X_ of size \(|X|\le\widetilde{O}(|A|^{1-\delta/2})\) such that \(A\subseteq X+X\). Such _X_ exists by a simple probabilistic argument: Pick random subsets \(Y\subseteq-A\) and \(Z\subseteq A+A\) with sizes \(|Y|,|Z|=\Theta(|A|^{1-\delta/2}\sqrt{log|A|})\) and let \(X=Y\cup Z\). Since each \(a\in A\) is represented as _a=y+z_ by at least |_A_| distinct pairs \((y,z)\in(-A)\times(A+A)\), with high probability at least one pair (_y,z_) survives in \(Y\cup Z\) for every \(a\in A\).

• _Clustered 3SUM._ Chan and Lewenstein \[CL15\] studied _clustered_ 3SUM, where a set is clustered if it can be covered by \(n^{1-\delta}\) intervals of length _n_ for some \(\delta>0\). They showed a truly subquadratic-time algorithm for this case. It is simple to show that if _A_ is clustered, then a low-rank decomposition of _A_ can be found efficiently: Let _S_ be the set of the smallest numbers in each of the intervals. Then notice that \(A\subseteq X+X\) where \(X=(S+\{0,1,\dots,n^{\delta/2}\})\cup\{n^{\delta/2},2n^{\delta/2},\dots,n\}\), which has size \(O(n^{1-\delta/2})\).<sup>6</sup><tbc>

<sup>4</sup>In \[EN77, BvHK25\], no explicit name is given for the measure in Definition 1.3. Our name _rank_ is inspired both from the connection to \[Fis26\], and since, coincidentally, the name \[2\]_-sumset rank_ has already been used in some previous work \[BFRV15\]. <sup>5</sup>A related problem, though significantly simpler, is to solve 3SUM when |_A+B_| or |_A-B_| is small; see \[BFN22, Fis24\]. <sup>6</sup>Chan and Lewenstein also studied a generalization of clustered 3SUM where the inputs are from Z_<sup>d</sup>_ for constant _d_. 3SUM with inputs from Z_<sup>d</sup>_ is essentially the same as 3SUM with integer inputs: Given a 3SUM instance with inputs from Z_<sup>d</sup>_, we can map each input vector to an integer by viewing the vector as the _d_-digit representation of the integer

## 1.4 Universe Reduction for Min-Plus Convolution

Having stated our two main technical innovations, let us finally turn to our results involving Min- Plus Convolution. We start with our universe reduction. Here, by _universe_ \[_u_\] we refer to the range of the entries in the sequences _A_ and _B_. Recall that the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis postulates that the min-plus convolution _A∗B_ of two given sequences _A,B_ cannot be computed in subquadratic time. In this hypothesis, as is common in fine-grained complexity, the assumption is that the universe is polynomially bounded, _u=n_<sup>_O_(1)</sup>. A stronger hypothesis, the _Strong_ Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis, postulates that subquadratic time is impossible even for sequences over the universe \[_n_\]:

**Hypothesis 1.5** (Strong Min-Plus Convolution)**.** _Min-Plus Convolution over the universe_ \[_n_\] _cannot be solved in time_ \(O(n^{2-\epsilon})\) _for any constant_ \(\epsilon>0\).

For even smaller universes, however, there are faster algebraic algorithms. Specifically, the Min- Plus Convolution problem can be reduced to computing the sumset of two integer sets in {0_,...,nu_}, leading to an alternative \(\widetilde{O}(nu)\)-time algorithm using the FFT. This algorithm differs substantially from the naive brute-force algorithm, suggesting that in this small-universe regime (\(u\checkmark n\)) the Min- Plus Convolution problem might behave quite differently than in the large-universe regime (\(u\gg n\)). Thus, a natural question is whether this \(\widetilde{O}(nu)\) could be improved, perhaps by some more elaborate algebraic technique? Investigating this question is also highly relevant for the Min-Plus Convolution problem as a source of hardness, as many lower bounds under the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis could be strengthened if we could assume hardness for small universes. We successfully resolve this question, proving that time \(\widetilde{O}(nu)\) is best-possible across all ranges of \(u\le n\):

**Theorem 1.6** (Small-Universe Reduction)**.** _Let_ \(\gamma\in[0,1]\)_. Min-Plus Convolution for length-n input sequences over a universe of size_ \(u=n^\gamma\) _cannot be solved in time_ \(O(n^{1+\gamma-\epsilon})\) _(for any constant_ \(\epsilon>0\)_), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails._

Even more ambitiously, can one also show a reduction from the large-universe regime? Is there a universe reduction from, say, _u=n_<sup>10</sup> to _u=n_? We _almost_ answer this question in the affirmative. Unfortunately, in analogy with \[Fis26\], there remains one key step in our proof for which the state-of-the-art additive combinatorics tools are not strong enough yet. For this reason, Fischer encapsulated the missing structural statement as the following plausible hypothesis. Let us call a function \(h:X\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}\) _sum-order-preserving_ if, for every \(x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2\in X\), _x_<sub>1</sub>+_x_<sub>2</sub>_\<y_<sub>1</sub>+_y_<sub>2</sub> implies _h(x_<sub>1</sub>)+_h(x_<sub>2</sub>)_\<h(y_<sub>1</sub>)+_h(y_<sub>2</sub>).

**Hypothesis 1.7** (\[Fis26\])**.** _There is a constant c such that the following holds. For every set of integers X with doubling_ \(|X+X|\le K|X|\)_, there is a subset_ \(Y\subseteq X\) _of size_ \(|Y|\ge|X|/K^c\) _and a sum-order-preserving function_ \(h:Y\rightarrow\{0,1,\dots,|X|\}\)_. Moreover, given X, one can compute Y and h in time_ |_X_|<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>_K_<sup>_O_(1)</sup>.

Intuitively, Hypothesis 1.7 speculates that every low-doubling integer set can be compressed to an interval in such a way that the order of pairwise sums is preserved. This statement is closely<tbc>

In the clustered case, when \(A\subseteq S+H\), where \(|S|\le n^{1-\delta}\) and _H_ is a hypercube of volume at most _n_, their algorithm also runs in truly subquadratic time. Similar as the integer case, we can write _H_ as the sum of _Y+Z_ where _Y_ has size \(O(n^\delta)\) and _Z_ has \(O(n^{1-\delta})\) (this is possible because _H_ is a hypercube). Hence, letting \(X=(S+Y)\cup Z\) guarantees that \(A\subseteq X+X\) and \(|X|\le O(n^{1-\delta/2})\).

Currently, the state-of-the-art bounds \[Rag25\] together with the work of \[ABC18\] imply that one can take exp((log_K_)<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>) instead of _K<sup>c</sup>_ in Hypothesis 1.7. We therefore hope that Hypothesis 1.7 will eventually be resolved alongside the PFR Conjecture. We refer to \[Fis26\] for a more detailed discussion of this hypothesis and its plausibility.

Under Hypothesis 1.7 we do obtain the full universe reduction:

**Theorem 1.8** (Large-Universe Reduction)**.** _Under Hypothesis 1.7, the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis and the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis are equivalent._

In summary, under Hypothesis 1.7, Theorems 1.6 and 1.8 fully characterize the complexity of Min-Plus Convolution as \(min\{n^2,nu\}^{1\pm o(1)}\) for all universe sizes \(u=n^{\Theta(1)}\). If this algorithm can be improved in any regime, then the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails.

## 1.5 Application to Intermediate Convolution Problems

Fischer \[Fis26\] also showed a list of APSP-based tight conditional lower bounds for "intermediate" problems, a well-studied class of matrix problems whose running times are about _n_<sup>2.5</sup> when \(\omega=2\). Likewise, our techniques also allow us to show matching conditional lower bounds for a range of intermediate sequence problems, whose best known running times are \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})\).

### Min-Max Convolution.

In the Min-Max Convolution problem, we are given sequences _A,B_ of length _n_, and need to compute a sequence _C_ where _C_\[_k_\]=min<sub>_i+j=k_</sub>max{_A_\[_i\],B_\[_j_\]}. Bringmann, Künnemann and Wegrzycki \[BKW19\] showed that this problem is equivalent to approximate Min- Plus Convolution. An \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})\) time algorithm for computing Min-Max Convolution was known as early as 1989 \[Kos89\]. However, no further improvements were known since then, and there is also no strong evidence why this running time might be optimal. We show a tight conditional lower bound for Min-Max Convolution.

**Theorem 1.9** (Min-Max Convolution)**.** _Min-Max Convolution cannot be solved in time_ \(O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})\) _(for any constant_ \(\epsilon>0\)_), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails._

### Min-Equality Convolution.

In the Min-Equality Convolution problem, we are given sequences _A,B_ of length _n_, and need to compute a sequence _C_ where

\(C[k]=min_{i+j=kA[i]=B[j]}A[i].\)

Previously, it was studied by Chan, Vassilevska Williams and Xu \[CVX23\], who showed that Min- Equality Convolution requires _n_<sup>12/11-_o_(1)</sup> time, under the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis (they also showed an _n_<sup>7/6-_o_(1)</sup> lower bound based on the Strong APSP Hypothesis and an _n_<sup>5/4-_o_(1)</sup> lower bound based on the unweighted directed APSP Hypothesis, but neither matches the \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})\) upper bound). In our work, we significantly improve their result, by showing a tight lower bound based on the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis.

**Theorem 1.10** (Min-Equality Convolution)**.** _Min-Equality Convolution cannot be solved in time_ \(O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})\) _(for any constant_ \(\epsilon>0\)_), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails._

#### Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution.

Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution is a version of Min-Plus Convolution with structured inputs. A length-_n_ sequence is called bounded monotone if all entries are from \[_O(n_)\], and the sequence is monotonically nondecreasing. Chan and Lewenstein \[CL15\] were the first to study Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution: they showed that when both input sequences are bounded monotone, Min-Plus Convolution can be computed in _O(n_<sup>1.859</sup>) time. This running time has been improved to \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})\) by Chi, Duan, Xie and Zhang \[CDXZ22\], and Bringmann, Dürr and Polak \[BDP24\] generalized their algorithm to the case where only one of the sequences needs to be bounded monotone. Bounded-Monotone Min-Plus Convolution has found a variety of applications, including Jumbled Indexing \[CL15\] and several variants of knapsack \[BC22, BDP24, CLMZ25\]. We show that \[BDP24\]’s algorithm is conditionally optimal:

**Theorem 1.11** (Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution)**.** _Min-Plus Convolution between an arbitrary sequence and a monotone sequence bounded by_ \[_n_\] _cannot be solved in time_ \(O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})\) _(for any constant_ \(\epsilon>0\)_), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails._

#### Min-Witness Convolution.

Given two length-_n_ Boolean sequences _A,B_, their Min-Witness Convolution _C_ is defined such as _C_\[_k_\] equals the minimum index _i_ where _A_\[_i_\] and _B_\[_k-i_\] are both true. This problem has been listed in papers studying fine-grained complexity of intermediate problems \[LPV20, CVX23\] as a natural target for proving conditional lower bound for, but there has been no nontrivial lower bound so far for this problem. We prove the first super-linear (albeit non-tight) conditional lower bound for Min-Witness Convolution:

**Theorem 1.12** (Min-Witness Convolution)**.** _Min-Witness Convolution cannot be solved in time_ \(O(n^{4/3-\epsilon})\) _(for any constant_ \(\epsilon>0\)_), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails._

A careful reader might have noticed that our lower bounds for intermediate sequence problems are based on the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis, while Fischer \[Fis26\]’s lower bounds for intermediate matrix problems are based on the APSP Hypothesis itself rather than its strong variant. Without relying on Hypothesis 1.7, Fischer first reduced APSP to a version of Min-Plus Product where the universe has low-doubling (rather than simply an interval \[_u_\]), and then obtained APSP-based lower bounds for intermediate matrix problems from this first step. We also manage to prove an analogous version of the first step in Min-Plus Convolution (Lemma 5.3); unfortunately, it seems hard to obtain tight reductions for intermediate sequence problems from it. Intuitively, one reason why it is harder to design reductions to intermediate sequence problems is the following: In Fischer’s universe reduction for APSP, both the inner dimension and the universe of the Min-Plus Product are reduced, which make it easier to further reduce to intermediate matrix problems. In contrast, for sequence problems, there is no analogue of an "inner dimension", so there is less room to work with in downstream reductions.

## 1.6 Proof Ideas

In this section we give a quick high-level overview for the results we have not sketched before.

### 1.6.1 Low-Rank 3SUM in Subquadratic Time

We start with the ideas behind our subquadratic-time algorithm for low-rank 3SUM. Let (_A,B,C_) denote a given 3SUM instance, and assume that \(C\subseteq X+X\) for some small set, \(|X|\le n^{1-\epsilon}\). At<tbc>

the heart of our algorithm lies a curious win-win paradigm: Either we can solve the instance by a clever brute-force algorithm, or we can _amplify_ structure.

Specifically, to find a 3SUM solution _a+b=c_ we could try to enumerate _all_ solutions<tbc>

\(a+b=x_1+x_2,\text{for}a\in A,b\in B,x_1,x_2\in X.\) (1)

<tbc>For each such solution we can test if _a+b=x_<sub>1</sub>+_x_<sub>2</sub> is actually an element in _C_; only then have we found a solution. This might seem like overkill--after all we are listing many more solutions than necessary. But the crucial advantage is that solutions to this equation can be listed very efficiently. Indeed, rewriting each solution as

\(a-x_1=x_2-b,\)

a natural meet-in-the-middle algorithm is to preprocess the sets _A-X_ and _X-B_ in time _O_(|_A_||_X_|+|_B_||_X_|)=\(O(n^{2-\epsilon})\). Afterwards, we can list all solutions in time _O(N_), where _N_ denotes the number of solutions. If \(N\le n^{2-\delta}\), say, then this algorithm runs in subquadratic time. But of course, _N_ might be much larger, possibly up to \(|X|^2n=n^{3-2\epsilon}\), and in that case the meet-in-the-middle strategy is doomed.

Our key insight is that, in this situation, the sets _A_ and _B_ admit amplified structure. Concretely, focus on _B_. For simplicity, assume that all elements \(b\in B\) participate in roughly the same number of solutions to Equation (1), i.e., in about _N/|B_| solutions. Then, in other words, each \(b\in B\) is an \(N/|B|\ge n^{1-\delta}\)-popular sum in the set _X+X-A_. Note that we started from the structural information that \(C\subseteq X+X\), but ended up with the information that _B_ is covered by the \(n^{1-\delta}\)- popular sums in _X+X-A_. It turns out that this argument can be iterated. By arguing as above, but exchanging the roles of _B_ and _C_, we can either solve the instance, or further derive that _C_ is covered by the \(n^{2-2\delta}\)-popular sums in _X+X-A+A_. And iterating this argument _k_ times, we eventually infer that _C_ is covered by the \(n^{2k-2k\delta}\)-popular sums in _X+X-kA+kA_.

At this point, _C_ witnesses an \(n^{2k-2k\delta}\)-popular sum in _X+X-kA+kA_. This is where our structure theorem (Theorem 1.2) comes into play. When carefully applied, it implies that there is some low-doubling set _H_ of size at about \(|X|^2n^{2k\delta}\le n^{2-2\epsilon+2k\delta}\) that covers a large fraction of _A_. Here, intuitively think of \(\delta\) as an extremely small constant, so that the \(2k\delta\) term effectively becomes 0. That is, intuitively, we have showed that _A_ is covered by a low-doubling set of size |_X_|<sup>2</sup>. All in all, it is quite intriguing _how_ the structure amplifies: We start from a weakly structured set _C_, then infer some more structure for _B_, then again for _C_, and so on. And eventually, we conclude that _A_ admits a small low-doubling container. Besides, it is interesting that for a 3SUM algorithm the relevant structure lies in the number of _k_-sums.

Of course, we are not completely done. What remains is a 3SUM instance (_A,B,C_) equipped with a container set \(H\supseteq A\) of size \(|H|\le n^{2-\epsilon}\) and with arbitrarily low doubling. But this instance can be dealt with following ideas that have already appeared in earlier work (notably, \[JX23\]), and for this reason we defer further details to Section 4.

## 1.6.2 Universe Reduction for Min-Plus Convolution

Finally, we give a brief glimpse into our new universe reduction. Only at this point will it become clear why the rank of a set is a reasonable notion in our context.

For concreteness, focus on the universe reduction from \[_n_\] to \([\sqrt{n}]\). That is, we argue that if Min-Plus Convolution over the universe \([\sqrt{n}]\) is in time \(O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})\), then Min-Plus Convolution over<tbc>

the universe \[_n_\] is in time \(O(n^{2-\epsilon^\prime})\) (contradicting the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis). Let _A,B_ denote the given length-_n_ sequences over the universe \[_n_\]. We rewrite the sequences into their base-\(\sqrt{n}\) representation as \(A=A_1\cdot q+A_0,\)
\(B=B_1\cdot q+B_0,\) where the four sequences _A_0_,B_0_,A_1_,B_1 are each over the universe \([\sqrt{n}]\). Let us call an index _i_ a _witness_ of _k_ if (_A∗B_)\[_k_\]=_A_\[_i_\]+_B_\[_k-i_\], and a _pseudo-witness_ if (_A_1∗_B_1)\[_k_\]=_A_1\[_i_\]+_B_1\[_k-i_\]. Equivalently, the pseudo-witnesses are those indices that would become indices when rounding _A,B_ to multiples of \(\sqrt{n}\). By standard approaches, we can assume _A_0 and _B_0 have entries less than \(\sqrt{n}/2\), so that a witness must be a pseudo-witness. We will now execute the structure-versus-randomness paradigm that we sketched in the beginning. The notion of _pseudo-randomness_ turns out to concern the number of pseudo-witnesses: in a pseudo-random instance, all indices _k_ have few pseudo-witnesses, say at most \(n^{1/2+\epsilon/2}\). This is indeed a good case for our reduction, as we can afford to list _all_ pseudo-witnesses. Notably, this list also contains the true witnesses. To obtain the list of pseudo-witnesses, we apply a simple sampling trick (Lemma 2.14), reducing the listing problem to \(\tilde{O}(n^{1/2+\epsilon/2})\) plain min-plus convolutions of restrictions of _A_1 and _B_1. These are sequences over the universe \([\sqrt{n}]\), and can thus be convolved in time \(O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})\) by our initial assumption. The total time is \(O(n^{2-\epsilon/2})\). Of course, we first need to transform the initial instance (_A,B_) into a pseudo-random one, and this is where the rank becomes relevant. To simplify in this overview, suppose that _all_ indices _k_ have many (i.e., more than \(n^{1/2+\epsilon/2}\)) pseudo-witnesses.7 In this case, so we claim, the whole instance has low rank and can directly be solved in subquadratic time. To see this, we first apply the standard reduction from Min-Plus Convolution to 3SUM: We approximate _C≈A∗B_ (by some standard trick, with coordinate-wise constant additive error), then replace the sequences _A,B,C_ by their _indexed sets_ \(\mathcal{A}=\{(i,A[i]):0\le i\le n\},\)
\(\mathcal{B}=\{(j,B[j]):0\le j\le n\},\)
\(\mathcal{C}=\{(k,C[k]):0\le k\le 2n\},\) and solve the remaining 3SUM instance (A,B,C). These are 2-dimensional sets that can be flattened to plain integers via the usual embedding. We argue that C has low rank, \(r(\mathcal{C})\le\tilde{O}(n^{1-\epsilon/4})\). This can be shown in two steps: • First, consider the set \(\mathcal{C}_1=\{(k,(A_1*B_1)[k]\cdot\sqrt{n}):0\le k\le 2n\}.\) Assuming that each _k_ has many pseudo-witnesses, we can sample a set of \(\tilde{O}(n^{3/4-\epsilon/4})\) indices \(X\subseteq[0,n]\). With good probability, for each _k_ we include some witness \(i\in X\) and simultaneously also \(k-i\in X\). In this case, the set \(\mathcal{X}_1=\{(i,A_1[i]\cdot\sqrt{n}):i\in X\}\cup\{(j,B_1[j]\cdot\sqrt{n}):j\in X\}\) satisfies \(\mathcal{C}_1\subseteq\mathcal{X}_1+\mathcal{X}_1\), witnessing that \(r(\mathcal{C}_1)\le|\mathcal{X}_1|\le O(n^{3/4-\epsilon/4})\). 7In fact, this idealized situation is impossible. For instance, _k_=0 always has exactly one (pseudo-)witness, namely _i_=0. But this is a technicality that shall not concern us in this overview.

• Second, note that C<sub>1</sub> is an indexed set that approximates C well. Indeed, for any \(c\in\mathcal{C}\), there exists \(c_1\in\mathcal{C}_1\) such that \(c-c_1\in\mathcal{I}\), where \(\mathcal{I}=\{(0,0),\dots,(0,\sqrt{n})\}\). Hence, we can expand X<sub>1</sub> to X so that \(\mathcal{X}_1+\mathcal{X}_1+\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathcal{X}+\mathcal{X}\), which will then imply \(\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{X}+\mathcal{X}\). To achieve this, we set<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_1\cup\left\{(0,0),(0,1),\dots,(0,n^{1/4})\right\}\cup\left\{(0,n^{1/4}),(0,2\cdot n^{1/4}),\dots,(0,\sqrt{n})\right\}.\)<tbc>

<tbc>Finally, \(r(\mathcal{C})\le|\mathcal{X}|\le O(n^{1-\epsilon/4})\).

In summary, our low-rank 3SUM algorithm (Theorem 4.1) can solve the 3SUM instance (A,B,C) in subquadratic time \(O(n^{2-\epsilon^\prime})\).

## 2 Preliminaries

We use \[_n_\] to denote {1,2_,...,n_} for any integer \(n\ge 0\).

### 2.1 Additive Combinatorics

For two sets \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\), define their _sumset_ \(A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\}\) and _difference set_ \(A-B=\{a-b:a\in A,b\in B\}\). Let \(-A=\{-a:a\in A\}\). The _k_-fold sumset _kA_ is recursively defined by _kA_=(_k_-1)_A+A_ with 1_A=A_. Denote \(r_{A+B}(z)=|\{(x,y)\in A\times B:x+y=z\}|\). We often conveniently refer to _r_<sub>_A+B_</sub>(_z_) as the _multiplicity_ of _z_ in the sumset _A+B_. Similarly, the _multiplicity_ of _z_ in the _k_-fold sumset _kA_ means \(|\{(x_1,\dots,x_k)\in A^k:x_1+\cdots+x_k=z\}|\).

**Lemma 2.1** (Plünnecke-Ruzsa Inequality)**.** _For two sets A,B, if_ \(|A+B|\le K|A|\)_, then for any integers_ \(n,m\ge 0\), \(|mB-nB|\le K^{m+n}|A|\).

**Lemma 2.2** (Sparse Convolution, \[BFN22\])**.** _There is a deterministic algorithm that, given_ \(A,B\subseteq[-u,u]\)_, computes the sumset A+B along with the multiplicities r_<sub>_A+B_</sub> _in time_ \(|A+B|\cdot(\mathrm{log}u)^{O(1)}\).

The _additive energy_ between two sets \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) is<tbc>

\(E(A,B)=|\{(a_1,a_2,b_1,b_2)\in A^2\times B^2:a_1+b_1=a_2+b_2\}|=\sum_zr_{A+B}(z)^2.\)

<tbc>The additive energy of a set \(A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) is _E(A_)=_E(A,A_). We also define the following standard higher-order analogue of the additive energy, for any integer \(k\ge 1\):

\(T_k(A)=|\{(a_1,\dots,a_k,b_1,\dots,b_k)\in A^{2k}:a_1+\cdots+a_k=b_1+\cdots+b_k\}|.\)

The Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers (BSG) Theorem was originally proved in \[BS94, Gow01\]. We use the following algorithmic version of the BSG theorem appearing in \[ABF23, Theorem 3.3\] (which is an adaptation of \[CL15\]).

**Theorem 2.3** (BSG Theorem)**.** _If set A has additive energy_ \(E(A)\ge|A|^3/K\)_, then there exists a subset_ \(A'\subseteq A\) _such that_

• \(|A'|\ge\Omega(K^{-2}|A|)\)_, and_<tbc>

• \(|A'+A'|\le O(K^{24}|A|)\).<tbc>

_Moreover, given A and K, we can compute_ \(A'\) _in time_ \(\widetilde{O}(K^{12}|A|)\) _by a randomized algorithm._

The Asymmetric BSG Theorem was proved in the textbook by Tao and Vu \[TV06, Section 2.6\]. We need an algorithmic version of this theorem stated below, which we prove in Section 7.

**Theorem 2.4** (Asymmetric BSG Theorem)**.** _Let_ \(\epsilon>0\) _and_ \(0<\alpha\le 1\)_. Let_ \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _be sets with energy_ \(E(A,B)\ge\alpha|A|^2|B|\)_. Then there are sets_ \(H,\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _and some_ \(K\le O_\epsilon(\alpha^{-O_\epsilon(1)}(1+|B|/|A|)^\epsilon)\) _such that:_

• \(|H+H|\le K|H|\),<tbc>

• \(|H||\Lambda|\le K|B|\),<tbc>

• \(|A\cap H|\ge|A|/K\) _and_ \(|B\cap(H+\Lambda)|\ge|B|/K\).

_Moreover, there is a randomized algorithm to compute_ \(H,\Lambda\) _in time_ \(\widetilde{O}((|A|+|B|)K)\).

Related to these tools, we will also need to compute approximations of sumset multiplicities.

**Lemma 2.5** (Approximating Sumset Multiplicities)**.** _There is a randomized algorithm that, given sets A,B,C and_ \(\epsilon>0\)_, computes approximations_ \(\tilde{r}(x)\)_, for all_ \(x\in C\)_, with additive error_

\(|r_{A+B}(x)-\tilde{r}(x)|\le\epsilon|A|.\)

_The algorithm runs in time_ \(\widetilde{O}(|A|+|B|/\epsilon+|C|)\).

A proof of Lemma 2.5 can be found in \[FJX25,  6\]. See \[FJX25, Corollary 3.1\] for a derandomization of this algorithm.

## 2.2 Problem Definitions

As is common in fine-grained complexity, hardness hypotheses and reductions implicitly allow Monte-Carlo randomization (though there has been some interest in derandomizing 3SUM-related reductions \[CH20, FKP24\]).

**Definition 2.6** (3SUM)**.** Given three sets of integers _A,B,C_, determine whether there exists \(a\in A,b\in B,c\in C\) such that _a+b=c_. In its All-Integer version we need to determine for every number in the input, whether it participates in a solution _a+b=c_.

We use 3SUM(_n_) to denote the running time of 3SUM instances with size-_n_ inputs. We also use \(3SUM(n|r\le R)\) to denote the running time of 3SUM instances where the rank (Definition 1.3) of one of the sets is at most _R_, and such a rank decomposition is given. A subinstance of a 3SUM instance with input (_A,B,C_) is another 3SUM instance with input \((A',B',C')\) where \(A'\subseteq A,B'\subseteq B,C'\subseteq C\).

**Definition 2.7** (Min-Plus Convolution)**.** Given two sequences \(A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}\), compute a sequence \(C=A*B\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,2n]}\), where _C_\[_k_\]=min<sub>_i+j=k_</sub>{_A_\[_i_\]+_B_\[_j_\]}.

We use MPConv(_n_) to denote the running time of Min-Plus Convolution instances with size-_n_ inputs. We also use \(MPConv(n|u\le U)\) to denote the running time of Min-Plus Convolution instances where the entries are from \[_U_\].

**Definition 2.8** (Min-Plus Convolution Listing)**.** Given two sequences \(A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}\), and an integer threshold _t_, list _t_ witnesses (_i,j_) where _A_\[_i_\]+_B_\[_j_\]=(_A∗B_)\[_k_\] for every _k_. If there are fewer than _t_ witnesses for certain indices _k_, list all the witnesses for these indices.

Similar as before, we use MPConvList(_n,t_) and \(\text{MPConvList}(n,t|u\le U)\) to denote the running times. A subinstance of Min-Plus Convolution (and all sequence problems considered in this paper) can be obtained by setting some entries to \(\perp\), a value that cannot be involved in any solution.

**Definition 2.9** (Bounded-Monotone Min-Plus Convolution)**.** Given two sequences \(A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}\) where _B_ is monotonically nondecreasing and has entries in \[_O(n_)\], compute _A∗B_.

**Definition 2.10** (Min-Max Convolution)**.** Given two sequences \(A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}\), compute a sequence \(C=\text{Min-Max}(A,B)\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,2n]}\), where _C_\[_k_\]=min<sub>_i+j=k_</sub>max{_A_\[_i_\]_,B_\[_j_\]}.

**Definition 2.11** (Min-Equality Convolution)**.** Given two sequences \(A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}\), compute a sequence \(C=\text{Min-Equal}(A,B)\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,2n]}\), where _C_\[_k_\]=min<sub>_i+j=k,A_\[_i_\]=_B_\[_j_\]</sub>_A_\[_i_\].

**Definition 2.12** (Min-Witness Convolution)**.** Given two Boolean sequences \(A,B\in\{0,1\}^{[0,n]}\), compute a sequence \(C=\text{Min-Witness}(A,B)\in(\mathbb{Z}\cup\{\perp\})^{[0,2n]}\), where \(C[k]=min\{i\in[0,n]:k-i\in[0,n]\wedge A[i]=B[k-i]=1\}\) (if no such _i_ exists, define \(C[k]=\perp\)).

We now define the index set of a sequence. We will frequently use this notion to convert Min-Plus Convolution instances to 3SUM instances.

**Definition 2.13** (Index set \(\mathcal{I}(\cdot)\))**.** For a sequence \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}\) indexed by integers in \[0_,n_\], the _index set_ of _A_ is \(\mathcal{I}(A)=\{(i,A[i]):i\in[0,n]\}\).

More generally, for a sequence \(A\in(\mathbb{Z}\cup\{\perp\})^{[0,n]}\), the index set of _A_ is \(\mathcal{I}(A)=\{(i,A[i]):i\in[0,n],A[i]\neq\perp\}\).

## 2.3 Reduction from Listing to Non-Listing Problems

For most problems considered in this paper, one can use an algorithm for the non-listing version of a problem to list witnesses, via a standard approach based on sampling and parallel binary search (e.g., \[AGMN92, Sei95\]). This is summarized in the following lemma.

**Lemma 2.14** (Listing Witnesses for Convolution Problems)**.** _Any Min-Plus Convolution Listing instance_ (_A,B_) _with threshold t can be reduced to t_(log_n_)<sup>_O_(1)</sup> _Min-Plus Convolution (non-Listing) subinstances. The reduction runs in time_ \(\widetilde{O}(nt)\)_. In particular,_

\(\text{MPConvList}(n,t|u)\le\widetilde{O}(t\cdot\text{MPConv}(n|u)).\)

_Moreover, for any_ \(t_1,t_2\ge 1\),

\(\text{MPConvList}(n,t_1t_2|u)\le\widetilde{O}(t_1\cdot\text{MPConvList}(n,t_2|u)).\)

_The same statements also hold with "Min-Plus" replaced by "Min-Max" and "Min-Equality"._

We omit the proof of Lemma 2.14 here since it is standard. We refer readers to \[Fis26, Section 5.1\] for a proof in the analogous setting of Min-Plus Matrix Product, which can be adapted to Min- Plus Convolution in a straightforward manner. The same proof strategy also applies to Min-Max Convolution and Min-Equality Convolution.<sup>8</sup>

The same sampling strategy together with FFT yields the following more well-known lemma for listing witnesses of Boolean Convolution:

**Lemma 2.15.** _Given two sequences_ \(A,B\in\{0,1\}^{[0,n]}\) _and a threshold_ \(t\ge 1\)_, one can compute their Boolean Convolution_ \(C\in\{0,1\}^{[0,2n]}\) _defined as_ \(C[k]=\vee_{i+j=k}(A[i]\wedge B[j])\)_, and additionally, for each k, list up to t witnesses i such that A_\[_i_\]=_B_\[_k-i_\]=1_, in_ \(\widetilde{O}(tn)\) _time._

## 3 Popular _k_-Sum Structure

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem 1.2. We start with some basic definitions and facts.

**Definition 3.1** (Popular _k_-Sums)**.** Let \(A_1,\dots,A_k\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\), and _p\>_0. The set Pop(_A_<sub>1</sub>_,...,A<sub>k</sub>;p_) consists of all integers _x_ that can be expressed in at least _p_ distinct ways as

\(x=a_1+\cdots+a_k\)

for \((a_1,\dots,a_k)\in A_1\times\cdots\times A_k\); we call these the _p-popular k-sums_. When \(A=A_1=\cdots=A_k\), we simply write Pop_<sup>k</sup>(A;p_).

The following simple observation will be useful later.

**Observation 3.2.** _If_ \(\mathrm{Pop}(A_1,\dots,A_k;p)\neq\emptyset\) _then_ \(\mathrm{Pop}(A_2,\dots,A_k;p/|A_1|)\neq\emptyset\).

**Theorem 1.2** (Popular _k_-Sums Imply Low-Doubling Structure)**.** _For every c\>_0 _and_ \(\epsilon>0\)_, there is some_ \(k=k(c,\epsilon)\) _such that the following holds. Let_ \(A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _and assume that_ \(\mathrm{Pop}^k(A;p)\neq\emptyset\) _for some_ \(p=\Omega(|A|^{k-1-c})\)_. Then there exists a set_ \(H\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _and some_ \(K=O_{c,\epsilon}(|A|^\epsilon)\) _such that:_

• \(|H|\le K|A|^{1+c}\),<tbc>

## 3.1 Qualitative Optimality

Let us briefly comment that Theorem 1.2 is (qualitatively) optimal. For every _c\>_0 and every integer \(k\ge 2\), there is a small enough \(\epsilon\in(0,1)\) that would violate the theorem statement. More specifically, there is a family of size-_n_ sets _A_ such that \(Pop^k(A;p)\neq\emptyset\) for some \(p=\Omega(|A|^{k-1-c})\), and so that any set _H_ with \(|A\cap H|\ge n^{1-\epsilon}\) and \(|H|\le n^{1+c+\epsilon}\) would have doubling constant much larger than \(n^\epsilon\). The same proof would also show for every \(\epsilon\in(0,1)\) and every \(k\ge 2\), there exists _c\>_0 that violates the theorem statement. This shows that _k_ in the theorem necessarily depends on _c_ and \(\epsilon\) (though the dependence could possibly be improved to linear in \(c/\epsilon\)).

Indeed, take _A=I+R_ where _I_ is an interval (or any other low-doubling set) of size _n_<sup>1-_c/_(_k_-1)</sup>, and where _R_ is a random set of size _n_<sup>_c/_(_k_-1)</sup> that is not correlated with _H_. By taking _R_ from a large enough universe, we can assume that, for every \(\ell\le(c+2)logn\), there is no \(\ell\)-term additive relation

\((i_1+r_1)+\cdots+(i_\ell+r_\ell)=(i_{\ell+1}+r_{\ell+1})+\cdots+(i_{2\ell}+r_{2\ell}),\)

where \(r_1,\dots,r_{2\ell}\) are distinct, while \(i_1,\dots,i_{2\ell}\) might not. Then _A_ has size roughly |_I_||_R_|=_n_. Moreover, Pop_<sup>k</sup>(A_;|_A_|<sup>_k_-1-_c_</sup>) is non-empty as each sum \(r_1+\cdots+r_k\in kR\) can be extended in about |_I_|<sup>_k_-1</sup>=_n_<sup>_k_-1-_c_</sup> ways to a common popular sum in _kI+kR_. Take _H_ to be any set where \(|H|\le n^{1+c+\epsilon}\) and \(|A\cap H|\ge n^{1-\epsilon}\). By pigeonhole principle, \(A\cap H\) must contain _p<sub>t</sub>=i<sub>t</sub>+r<sub>t</sub>_ for \(i_t\in I,r_t\in R\) where the values _r<sub>t</sub>_ are distinct, for some \(t\ge n^{1-\epsilon}/n^{1-c/(k-1)}=n^{c/(k-1)-\epsilon}\). By our assumption on _R_, there is no \(\ell\)-term additive relation for numbers _P_={_p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,p<sub>t</sub>_} for every \(\ell\le(c+2)logn\).

Now consider the additive energy _E(P,H_). For every nontrivial solution, _p_<sub>1</sub>+_h_<sub>1</sub>=_p_<sub>2</sub>+_h_<sub>2</sub> for \(p_1,p_2\in P\) and \(h_1,h_2\in H\), we consider adding an edge between _h_<sub>1</sub> and _h_<sub>2</sub>. Note that an \(\ell\)-cycle in this graph induces an \(\ell\)-term additive relation for numbers _P_. Hence, the girth of this graph is _\>(c_+2)log_n_, which implies that the number of edges is _O_(|_H_|) by the graph Moore bound \[AHL02\]. Hence, _E(P,H_) is dominated by the trivial solutions, so _E(P,H_)=_O_(|_P_||_H_|).

By Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

\(|P+H|=\sum_z[r_{P+H}(z)>0]\ge\frac{(\sum_zr_{P+H}(z))^2}{\sum_zr_{P+H}(z)^2}\ge\frac{|P|^2|H|^2}{O(|P||H|)}\ge\Omega(|P||H|).\)

As \(|H+H|\ge|P+H|\), the doubling constant of _H_ is at least \(\Omega(|P|)=\Omega(n^{c/(k-1)})\), which is greater than \(n^\epsilon\) when \(k\checkmark\frac{c}{\epsilon}\).

We finally revisit the previous proof to demonstrate that all steps can be implemented efficiently, leading to the following algorithmic theorem:

**Theorem 3.5.** _For every c\>_0 _and_ \(\epsilon>0\)_, there is some_ \(k=k(c,\epsilon)\) _such that the following holds. **Proof of Lemma 3.6.** Following the proof of Lemma 3.4, we design a recursive algorithm. ## 4 Subquadratic-Time Algorithm for Low-Rank 3SUM

In this section we design a subquadratic-time algorithm for low-rank 3SUM.

**Theorem 4.1** (Low-Rank 3SUM)**.** _For every_ \(0<\rho\le 1/2\) _there is some_ \(\delta=\delta(\rho)>0\) _such that the following holds. There is a randomized algorithm that solves a given All-Integer 3SUM instance_ (_A,B,C), when additionally provided with a set_ \(X\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _of size_ \(|X|\le n^{1-\rho}\) _satisfying_ \(A\subseteq X+X\)_, and runs in time_

\(3SUM(n|r\le n^{1-\rho})=O(n^{2-\delta}).\)

We will prove Theorem 4.1 by a sequence of two reduction steps to reduce from any given low- rank instance to few instances exhibiting even more structure. That structure is that the sets _A,B,C_ are all contained in some larger set _H_ with small doubling. For ease of notation we will typically refer to _H_ as a _low-doubling container_, formally defined as follows.

**Definition 4.2** (Low-Doubling Container)**.** We say that _H_ is a (_K,N)-container_ of some set _A_ if

• \(A\subseteq H\),<tbc>

• \(|H+H|\le K|H|\), and<tbc>

• \(|H|\le N\).

Our reduction can then be phrased as follows:

**Lemma 4.3** (From Low Rank to Low-Doubling Containment)**.** _For every_ \(\epsilon>0\) _and_ \(0<\rho\le 1/2\) _there is some_ \(\delta=\delta(\rho,\epsilon)>0\) _such that the following holds. There is a randomized algorithm that, given a 3SUM instance_ (_A,B,C_) _and a set X of size_ \(|X|\le n^{1-\rho}\) _such that_ \(C\subseteq X+X\)_, computes_

• \(O(n^\epsilon)\) _subinstances_ \((A'\subseteq A,B'\subseteq B,C'\subseteq C)\)_, each provided with a_ \((O(n^\epsilon),O(n^{2-2\rho}))\)_-container of_ \(A'\cup B'\cup C'\)_, and_

• _a set of 3SUM solutions_ \(\mathcal{T}\subseteq A\times B\times C\),

_so that each solution is either part of exactly one subinstance or part of_ T _. The algorithm runs in time_ \(O(n^{2-\delta})\).

We devote the following two subsections to the proof of Lemma 4.3. Once established, the proof of Theorem 4.1 is almost immediate by the following simple lemma.

**Lemma 4.4** (3SUM for Small Sumsets)**.** _Any All-Integer 3SUM instance_ (_A,B,C_) _with universe_ \[_u_\] _can be solved in deterministic time_ (|_A+B_|+|_B-C_|+|_A-C_|)(log_u_)<sup>_O_(1)</sup>.

**Proof.** To detect all elements in _C_ that are part of a solution, we compute the sumset _A+B_ by a sparse convolution in time |_A+B_|(log_u_)<sup>_O_(1)</sup> by Lemma 2.2, and report all elements in \(C\cap(A+B)\). To detect all elements in _A_ and _B_ that are part of a solution, we proceed similarly with _A_ and _B_ in place of _C_.

**Proof of Theorem 4.1.** Let \(\epsilon>0\) be a parameter to be determined. We apply Lemma 4.3 to the given instance (_A,B,C_) (by relabeling the input sets, we may assume _C_ has a low-doubling container as required by Lemma 4.3), and obtain \(O(n^\epsilon)\) subinstances \((A',B',C')\) and some set of 3SUM solutions T , with the promise that each solution in (_A,B,C_) either appears in a subinstance or in T . We report all items present in T . Then we solve all subinstances by Lemma 4.4, and further report all items that appear in a solution in at least one subinstance. The correctness is clear.

It remains to analyze the running time. The call to Lemma 4.3 takes time \(O(n^{2-\delta})\) for some constant \(\delta=\delta(\rho,\epsilon)>0\). We can also charge the scan through T to that running time. By Lemma 4.3, each constructed subinstance \((A',B',C')\) admits an \((K=O(n^\epsilon),N=O(n^{2-2\rho}))\)-container _H_ of \(A'\cup B'\cup C'\). It follows that<tbc>

\(|A'+B'|\le|H+H|\le K|H|\le O(n^{2-2\rho+\epsilon}).\)

<tbc>Similarly, by an application of the Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality (Lemma 2.1),

\(|B'-C'|\le|H-H|\le K^2|H|\le O(n^{2-2\rho+2\epsilon}).\)

Therefore, the \(O(n^\epsilon)\) calls to Lemma 4.4 run in total time \(O(n^{2-2\rho+3\epsilon})\). The claimed running time follows, picking any constant \(0<\epsilon<2\rho/3\).

## 4.1 Low-Doubling Containment for One Set

The proof of Lemma 4.3 involves two steps: (1) to reduce from any low-rank instance to subinstances where only one of the three sets admits a low-doubling container, and (2) to extend that one low- doubling container to all three sets. We start with step (1):

**Lemma 4.5** (Low-Doubling Containment for One Set)**.** _For every_ \(\epsilon>0\) _and_ \(0<\rho\le 1/2\) _there is some_ \(\delta=\delta(\rho,\epsilon)>0\) _such that the following holds. There is a randomized algorithm that, given a 3SUM instance_ (_A,B,C_) _and a set X of size_ \(|X|\le n^{1-\rho}\) _such that_ \(C\subseteq X+X\)_, computes_

• \(O(n^\epsilon)\) _subinstances_ \((A'\subseteq A,B,C)\) _with_ \(O(n^\epsilon)\)_-doubling_ \(O(n^{2-2\rho})\)_-containers of_ \(A'\)_, and_<tbc>

• _a set of 3SUM solutions_ \(\mathcal{T}\subseteq A\times B\times C\),

_so that each solution is either part of exactly one subinstance or part of_ T _. The algorithm runs in time_ \(O(n^{2-\delta})\).

The proof of Lemma 4.5 requires some setup. We start with the following simple lemma that allows to trade off the size of the container with its doubling.

**Lemma 4.6.** _Let_ \(\epsilon,\gamma>0\) _and_ \(0<\rho\le 1/2\)_. Then the 3SUM instance (_A,B,C_) is equivalent to the instances (_A_<sub>1</sub>_,B,C),...,(A<sub>t</sub>,B,C_) (in the sense that their solutions stand in one-to-one correspondence). Moreover, each _A<sub>i</sub>_ is contained in _H<sub>i</sub>_, and as

\(|H_i+H_i|\le|H+H|\le K|H|\le O(Kt)|H_i|=O(n^{\epsilon+\gamma})|H_i|,\)

_H<sub>i</sub>_ is a \((O(n^{\epsilon+\gamma}),O(n^{2-2\rho}))\)-container of _A<sub>i</sub>_.

The more interesting ingredient to Lemma 4.5 is the following lemma. Intuitively, it states that certain structure can be _amplified_. Namely, any 3SUM instance (_A,B,C_) where _C_ is a subset of (_k_+1)-popular sums can be replaced by a subinstance that is a subset of (_k_+2)-popular sums. Curiously, the amplified structure does not show up in _C_, but in _B_.

**Lemma 4.7.** _There is a randomized algorithm that, given a 3SUM instance_ (_A,B,C_) _and integer parameters_ \(p,s\ge 1\) _and sets_ \(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_k\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _satisfying_ \(C\subseteq Pop(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_k;p)\)_, computes_

• _a subinstance_ \((A,B'\subseteq B,C)\) _so that_ \(B'\subseteq Pop(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_k,-A;p')\) _for_ \(p'=p|A|/s\)_, and_<tbc>

• _a set of 3SUM solutions_ \(\mathcal{T}\subseteq A\times B\times C\),<tbc>

<tbc>_so that each solution is either part of the subinstance or part of_ T _. The algorithm runs in time_<tbc>

\(\widetilde{O}\big(\frac{s|X||Y_1|\dots|Y_k|}{p}+|A||X|+\frac{|B||Y_1|\dots|Y_k|}{p}+\frac{|A||B|}{s}\big).\)

<tbc>**Proof.** Let \(p'=p|A|/s\). We run Lemma 3.3 to compute a set _P_ satisfying

\(Pop(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_k,-A;2p')\subseteq P\subseteq Pop(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_k,-A;p').\)

We call an item \(b\in B\) _popular_ if \(b\in P\) and _unpopular_ otherwise, and deal with the unpopular and popular items separately.

• _(Unpopular Items)_ Our strategy is to list all solutions _a+b=c_ involving an unpopular item _b_. Let \(Y\subseteq Y_1+\cdots+Y_k\) be the set obtained by sampling some tuples \((y_1,\dots,y_k)\in Y_1\times\cdots\times Y_k\) uniformly at random with rate min(1_,R/p_) for some \(R=\Theta(logn)\); for each such tuple we insert the sum \(y_1+\cdots+y_k\) into _Y_ . Then we run a meet-in-the-middle algorithm to explicitly list all solutions<tbc>

<tbc>\(a+b=x+y\)<tbc>

<tbc>with \((a,b,x,y)\in A\times(B\backslash P)\times X\times Y\) . Note that this condition is equivalent to<tbc>

<tbc>\(a-x=y-b,\)<tbc>

<tbc>an application of "Fredman’s trick" \[Fre76\]. More specifically, enumerate all pairs \((a,x)\in A\times X\), and store each pair in a hash table (with collision lists) indexed by _a-x_. Then we enumerate all unpopular \(b\in B\backslash P\) and all \(y\in Y\) , and further list all entries (_a,x_) in the hash table at index _y-b_. For each 4-tuple (_a,b,x,y_) listed in this way we test if \(a+b\in C\). We will show that this algorithm indeed lists any 3SUM solution involving an unpopular item.<tbc>

• _(Popular Items)_ The only 3SUM solutions not listed in the previous step are those involving a popular item _b_, i.e., the solutions of the subinstance \((A,B',C)\) for \(B'=B\cap P\). Recall that also \(B'\subseteq Pop(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_k,-A;p')\) by construction.

## Correctness.

We show that the first case of the algorithm indeed lists all solutions _a+b=c_ involving an unpopular item _b_. From the initial assumption \(C\subseteq Pop(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_k;p)\) we get that _c_ can be expressed in at least _p_ ways as

\(c=x+y_1+\cdots+y_k,\)

for \(x\in X\) and \(y_i\in Y_i\). Each such representation corresponds to a unique tuple (_y_<sub>1</sub>_,...,y<sub>k</sub>_) (as each such tuple uniquely determines _x_ via \(x=c-y_1-\cdots-y_k\)). By construction of _Y_ , with high probability \(1-exp(-O(R))=1-1/n^{\Omega(1)}\), at least one such tuple (_y_<sub>1</sub>_,...,y<sub>k</sub>_) is present in _Y_ in the form \(y=y_1+\cdots+y_k\). In particular, _c_ can be expressed as _c=x+y_ for some \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y\) , and therefore there is a solution _a+b=x+y_. This solution is detected by the algorithm, and the correctness follows.

## Running Time.

The initial call to Lemma 3.3 takes time \(\widetilde{O}(|X||Y_1|\dots|Y_k||A|/p')\). In the un popular case, the construction of _Y_ takes time \(O(|Y|)=O(|Y_1|\dots|Y_k|\cdot R/p)\) (which will turn out to be negligible). The meet-in-the-middle algorithm takes time _O_(|_A_||_X_|) to prepare the hash table, plus time _O_(|_B_||_Y_|) to enumerate all pairs (_a,x_). To bound the total time of listing all 4-tuples (_a,b,x,y_), note that each unpopular item _b_ can be represented in at most \(2p'\) ways as

\(b=x+y_1+\cdots+y_k-a.\)

For each such representation, the tuple (_y_<sub>1</sub>_,...,y<sub>k</sub>_) is part of _Y_ only with probability _R/p_, and thus the total number of solutions _a=x+y-b_ is at most \(O(p'\cdot R/p)=O(|A|/s\cdot R)\) (in expectation and with high probability) for any unpopular _b_. In particular, the algorithm lists at most \(O(|B||A|/s\cdot R)\) such solutions overall. The popular case runs in linear time.

We are finally ready to prove Lemma 4.5.

## Proof of Lemma 4.5.

Let \(c=1-2\rho+3\epsilon\) and let \(k=k(c,\epsilon)\) be the constant from Theorem 3.5. Note that the statement of Lemma 4.3 allows us to arbitrarily decrease \(\epsilon\); all parts of the lemma benefit from smaller \(\epsilon\), except for the non-explicit dependence of \(\delta\). For convenience we will therefore decrease \(\epsilon\) whenever convenient.

## Step 1: Removing Popular _k_-Sums.

We will first repeatedly remove elements from _A_ until it contains no more popular _k_-sums/differences. More precisely, we will ensure that \(\mathrm{Pop}^k(\pm A;p)=\emptyset\) for \(p:=|A|^{k-1-c}\).

Run Theorem 3.5 on \(\pm A\) with parameter _p_, leading to one of two possible outcomes. If it certifies that \(\mathrm{Pop}^k(\pm A;p)=\emptyset\), then step 1 is complete and we move on to step 2. Otherwise, Theorem 3.5 identifies a subset \(A'\subseteq A\) of size \(|A'|\ge|A|/K\) along with a _K_-doubling \(K|A|^{2-2\rho+3\epsilon}\)-container of \(A'\), for some \(K=O(|A|^\epsilon)\). In this event we take \((A',B,C)\) as one of the constructed subinstances (the container is not quite as claimed; we deal with this issue in a moment). We then remove \(A'\) from _A_, and repeat the execution of step 1.

All in all, there can be at most \(\widetilde{O}(|A|^\epsilon)\) repetitions as each repetition removes \(\Omega(|A|^{1-\epsilon})\) elements from _A_. In particular, the number of constructed subinstances is \(\widetilde{O}(|A|^\epsilon)\), and each subinstance is \(O(|A|^\epsilon)\)-doubling \(O(|A|^{2-2\rho+4\epsilon})\)-contained. By Lemma 4.6 (applied with \(t=|A|^{4\epsilon}\)) we can further refine these subinstances to \(O(|A|^{5\epsilon})\) instances that are \(\widetilde{O}(|A|^{5\epsilon})\)-doubling \(O(|A|^{2-2\rho})\)-contained. This is as claimed when reducing \(\epsilon\) by a constant.

## Step 2: Small Sets.

Next, we easily assert that \(n\le|A|^{1+\epsilon}\). Otherwise we can solve the whole instance trivially in time \(n^{2-\Omega(\epsilon)}\), and report the set of solutions T .

## Step 3: Popular _k_-Sum Covers.

Once we reach this step, we will exhaustively list all 3SUM solutions. Let T be initially empty. We will successively remove elements from _B_ and _C_, while maintaining the invariant that each 3SUM solution that is eliminated in this way has already been listed in T . The algorithm runs in iterations \(\ell=1,\dots,k\). We also maintain the second invariant that, before the \(\ell\)-th iteration,

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
B\subseteq\mathrm{Pop}(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_\ell;p_\ell) & \text{if}\ell\text{is even}, \\
C\subseteq\mathrm{Pop}(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_\ell;p_\ell) & \text{if}\ell\text{is odd}.
\end{array}\right.\)

To satisfy this invariant initially (for \(\ell=1\)) we pick _Y_1=_X_ and _p_1=1; indeed, then the invariant follows from the assumption \(C\subseteq X+X\). Let \(s=|A|^{\epsilon/k}\). Each iteration depends on the parity of \(\ell\): • _If_ \(\ell\) _is odd:_ Apply Lemma 4.7 on the 3SUM instance (_A,B,C_), with parameters \(p_\ell\) and _s_ and sets \(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_\ell\); the invariant makes sure that the premise \(C\subseteq Pop(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_\ell;p_\ell)\) is fulfilled. This yields a set of solutions \(\mathcal{T}'\) and a subinstance \((A,B'\subseteq B,C)\). We update: \(\mathcal{T}:=\mathcal{T}\cup\mathcal{T}',\)
\(B:=B',\)
\(Y_{\ell+1}:=-A,\)
\(p_{\ell+1}:=\frac{p_\ell|A|}{s}.\) Lemma 4.7 states that each 3SUM solution is either in \(\mathcal{T}'\) or part of the instance \((A,B',C)\). Thus, after the update each solution is either in T or part of the instance (_A,B,C_), and therefore the first invariant is maintained. Lemma 4.7 also guarantees that \(B'\subseteq Pop(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_\ell,-A;p_\ell|A|/s)\). After the update, this precisely maintains the second invariant. • _If_ \(\ell\) _is even:_ Observe that our 3SUM instance (_A,B,C_) is equivalent to the appropriately transposed instance (_A,-C,-B_), i.e., their solutions stand in one-to-one correspondence. Apply Lemma 4.7 on (_A,-C,-B_) with parameters \(p_\ell\) and _s_ and sets \(-X,-Y_1,\dots,-Y_\ell\); the premise \(-B\subseteq Pop(-X,-Y_1,\dots,-Y_\ell;p_\ell)\) is satisfied by our invariant. This yields a set of solutions \(\mathcal{T}'\) and a subinstance \((A,C'\subseteq-C,-B)\). We update: \(\mathcal{T}:=\mathcal{T}\cup\{(a,b,c):(a,-c,-b)\in\mathcal{T}'\},\)
\(C:=-C',\)
\(Y_{\ell+1}:=A,\)
\(p_{\ell+1}:=\frac{p_\ell|A|}{s}.\) Similarly to before, Lemma 4.7 states that each transposed 3SUM solution is either in \(\mathcal{T}'\) or part of the instance \((A,C',-B)\). Thus, after the update each original solution is either in T or part of the instance (_A,B,C_), and therefore the first invariant is maintained. Lemma 4.7 also guarantees that \(C'\subseteq Pop(-X,-Y_1,\dots,-Y_\ell,-A;p_\ell|A|/s)\). After the update, this precisely maintains the second invariant. Once the final _k_-th iteration is complete, we report the set T and the subinstances constructed in step 1. This completes the description of the algorithm. ## Correctness. The correctness of steps 1 and 2 is fairly obvious; the interesting part is to argue that in step 3 we exhaustively list all solutions of (_A,B,C_). The key correctness claim is that once the _k_-th iteration terminates, _B_ or _C_ must be empty. Suppose otherwise that both are non-empty. Then our invariant implies that \(Pop(X,Y_1,\dots,Y_{k+1};p_{k+1})\neq\emptyset.\)

Recall that we picked _p_1=1 and \(p_{\ell+1}=p_\ell|A|/s\), and thus \(p_{k+1}=\frac{|A|^k}{s^k}.\) Moreover, we picked _Y_1=_X_ and \(Y_2,\dots,Y_{k+1}\subseteq\pm A\). For \(1\le\ell\le k\), the \(\ell\)-th iteration is dominated by the call to Lemma 4.7. Then let \(\delta=\mathrm{min}(\delta_0,\delta_1,\rho/2)\), and the proof is complete. ## 4.2 Low-Doubling Containment for All Sets Next, we demonstrate that low-doubling containment for one set can be extended to low-doubling containment for all three sets:

\(\hat{j}=(j\cdot 2n+B_1[j])\mathrm{mod}p,\)
\(\hat{k}=(k\cdot 2n+A_1[i]+B_1[j])\mathrm{mod}p.\) We now argue that three success events happen simultaneously with good probability. First, \(P[\hat{i}]=A_0[i]\), unless there is a collision of the form \(i\cdot 2n+A_1[i]\equiv i'\cdot 2n+A_1[i'](\mathrm{mod}p)\). By the Prime Number Theorem, for any fixed \(i'\) (distinct from _i_) this collision takes place only

with probability \(O(\hat{p}^{-1}\mathrm{log}u)\). This is at most 1/4_n_ by choosing the constant in \(\hat{p}\) sufficiently large. Taking a union bound over all _n_ choices of \(i'\), it follows that we avoid all collisions with probability at least 3/4. Second, we analogously have \(Q[\hat{j}]=B_0[j]\) with probability at least 3/4.

The third success event is that the only indices \(i',j'\), anchored in \(X_\ell\) and \(Y_\ell\), respectively, and satisfying<tbc>

\((i'+j')\cdot 2n+A_1[i']+B_1[j']\equiv\hat{k}(\mathrm{mod}p),\)

<tbc>are those for which \(i'+j'=i+j=k\) and \(A_1[i']+B_1[j']=A_1[i]+B_1[j]\). To analyze this event, note that \((i'+j')\cdot 2n+A_1[i']+B_1[j']\) takes only \(O(|\mathcal{A}_\ell+\mathcal{B}_\ell|\Delta_X\Delta_Y)\) distinct values. Each undesired value, i.e., each value other than \((i+j)\cdot 2n+A_1[i]+B_1[j]\), collides with \(\hat{k}\) (modulo _p_) with probability at most \(O(\hat{p}^{-1}\mathrm{log}u)\), and thus the error probability is

\(O\big(\frac{|\mathcal{A}_\ell+\mathcal{B}_\ell|\Delta_X\Delta_Y\mathrm{log}u}{\hat{p}}\big)=O\big(\frac{\alpha^{-5}t^3|X|\Delta_X\Delta_Y\mathrm{log}u}{\hat{p}}\big)=O\big(\frac{\alpha^{-5}t^3n\Delta_Y\mathrm{log}u}{\hat{p}}\big),\)

by Property (ii) of Theorem 5.7. Choosing the constant in \(\hat{p}\) sufficiently large, this error probability is at most 1/4, say.

All three success events happen simultaneously with probability at least 1/4. In this case we have \((P*Q)[\hat{k}]\le P[\hat{i}]+Q[\hat{j}]=A_0[i]+B_0[j]\) by the first two events, and

\((P*Q)[\hat{k}]\ge\mathrm{min}\{A_0[i']+B_0[j']:i'+j'=k,A_1[i']+B_1[j']=A_1[i]+B_1[j]\}\)

by the third event. Put together, it follows that \((P*Q)[\hat{k}]=A_0[i]+B_0[j]\), and that any witness \(\hat{i}\) corresponds to a witness \(i'\) of _k_. Consequently, we correctly set _C_\[_k_\]. Over the 100log_n_ iterations this event happens at least once with high probability.

### Running Time.

We finally analyze the running time. Suppose that Min-Plus Convolution over the universe \[_u_\] is in time \(O(n^{2-\epsilon})\) for some \(\epsilon>0\).

The heavy step runs in time \(O(n^{2-\delta})\). The light step first applies the BSG Covering theorem (Theorem 5.7) in time \(\widetilde{O}(|X|^2)=\widetilde{O}(n^{2-2\delta})\). We then enumerate all pairs in the remainder R, and for each such pair further enumerate \(\Delta_X^2\) pairs of indices amounting to time \(O(|\mathcal{R}|\Delta_X^2)=O(\alpha|X|^2\Delta_X^2)=O(\alpha n^2)=O(n^{2-\delta})\), by Property (iii) of Theorem 5.7. We then enumerate all \(m=O(\alpha^{-1})=O(n^\delta)\) pairs of sets \(\mathcal{A}_\ell,\mathcal{B}_\ell\), where the upper bound is due to Property (ii) of Theorem 5.7, and run _O_(log_n_) repetitions of the randomized construction. In each repetition we construct and solve a length-\(\Theta(\hat{p})\) instance of Min-Plus Convolution. Each such instance can be trivially split into \(\lceil\hat{p}/n\rceil^2\) subinstances of length at most _n_. The total time to solve these instances is

\(\widetilde{O}\big(m\cdot\frac{\hat{p}^2}{n^2}\cdot n^{2-\epsilon}\big)=\widetilde{O}\big(\alpha^{-11}t^6\Delta_Y^2\cdot n^{2-\epsilon}\big)=\widetilde{O}(n^{2+27\delta-\epsilon}).\)

Choosing \(\delta=\epsilon/28>0\), the total running time becomes \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2-\delta})\). This is truly subquadratic as claimed.

## 5.4 Large-Universe Reduction

We are finally in the position to complete the large-universe reduction:

**Lemma 5.8** (Large-Universe Reduction for Min-Plus Convolution)**.** _Assume Hypothesis 1.7. If Min-Plus Convolution over the universe_ \[_n_\] _can be solved in time_ \(O(n^{2-\epsilon})\) _for some constant_ \(\epsilon>0\)_, then Min-Plus Convolution over the universe_ \[_u_\] _can be solved in time_ \(O(n^{2-\epsilon^\prime}(\mathrm{log}u)^{O(1)})\) _for some constant_ \(\epsilon'>0\).

In other words, Lemma 5.8 states that the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis implies the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis assuming Hypothesis 1.7. This proves Theorem 1.8.

For the proof we will also rely on the following simple covering lemma, which essentially constitutes an instance of the classic greedy algorithm for Set Cover. For a proof see, e.g., \[Fis26, Lemma 5.11\].

**Lemma 5.9** (Greedy Covering)**.** _There is a deterministic algorithm that, given sets_ \(X,Y\subseteq[-u,u]\)_, computes a set_ \(S\subseteq[-2u,2u]\) _of size at most_ \(|Y-X|/|Y|\cdot\mathrm{ln}|X|\) _such that_ \(X\subseteq Y+S\)_. It runs in time_ \(|Y-X||S|\cdot(\mathrm{log}u)^{O(1)}\).

**Proof of Lemma 5.8.** Let \(\rho,\epsilon>0\) be two constants to be determined. We apply Lemma 5.3 to reduce any given Min-Plus Convolution instance over the universe \[_u_\] to \(O(n^\epsilon)\) instances of Min-Plus Convolution Listing with listing threshold \(t=O(n^{2\rho})\). Each such instance \((A',B')\) is equipped with a \((K=O(n^\epsilon),N=O(n^{2-2\rho}))\)-container _H_ for the joint index set \(\mathcal{I}(A')\cup\mathcal{I}(B')\). Focus on one such instance \((A',B')\) for now.

Let \(\phi:\mathbb{Z}^2\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}\) be the map defined by \(\phi(i,a)=i\cdot 10M+a\), where _M_ is an upper bound on the largest entry in _H_. Recall that \(H\subseteq[2n]\times\mathbb{Z}\), and that _H_ has doubling at most _K_. It follows easily that \(\phi\), restricted to _H+H_, is an isomorphism, and thus \(\phi(H)\) also has doubling at most _K_. Thus, we may apply Hypothesis 1.7 on the integer set \(\phi(H)\). This yields a subset \(Y\subseteq\phi(H)\) of size at least<tbc>

\(|Y|\ge\Omega\big(\frac{|H|}{K^c}\big),\)

<tbc>and a sum-order-preserving hash function \(h:Y\rightarrow\{0,\dots,N\}\), where _c_ is the constant from Hypothesis 1.7. Next, apply Lemma 5.9 to compute a set of shifts _S_ such that \(\phi(H)\subseteq Y+S\) and such that

\(|S|\le\frac{|Y-\phi(H)|}{|Y|}\cdot\mathrm{ln}|H|=O\big(K^c\cdot\frac{|\phi(H)-\phi(H)|}{|H|}\cdot\mathrm{log}|H|\big)=O(K^{c+2}\mathrm{log}|H|),\)

where the last step is due to the Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality (Lemma 2.1).

Next, we apply Lemma 2.14 to reduce the Min-Plus Convolution Listing instance \((A',B')\) with listing threshold \(t=O(n^{2\rho})\) to \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2\rho})\) plain Min-Plus Convolution subinstances (i.e., for which we do not have to list multiple witnesses). In what follows, fix any such instance, denoted (_A,B_); we argue that it reduces to few instances of Monotone Min-Plus Convolution over the universe \[_n_<sup>2</sup>\]. By Lemma 5.6, any such instance further reduces to (non-Monotone) Min-Plus Convolution over the universe \[_n_\]. Let _C_ be the output sequence, initialized to \(\perp\). We will only update _C_ by updates of the form \(C[k]\leftarrow\mathrm{min}\{C[k],A[i]+B[k-i]\}\), guaranteeing that no output is underestimated.

Enumerate all shifts \(s,t\in S\). For each pair, construct the sequences \(A_s,B_t\in([0,N]\cup\{\perp\})^{[0,n]}\) defined by \(A_s[i]=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } h(\phi(i,A[i])-s) & \text{if}\phi(i,A[i])\in Y+s, \\ \perp & \text{otherwise,} \end{array}\right.\)
\(B_t[j]=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } h(\phi(j,B[j])-t) & \text{if}\phi(j,B[j])\in Y+t, \\ \perp & \text{otherwise.} \end{array}\right.\) Note that both sequences are almost monotone: The sequence \(\phi(i,A[i])\) is increasing for _i_=0_,...,n_ (when restricted to the non-\(\perp\) entries), and hence, so are the images of \(\phi(i,A[i])-s\in Y\) under the order-preserving function _h_. To remove the \(\perp\) entries simply replace both sequences by their suffix-minima, i.e., replace _As_ and _Bt_ by \(A'_s[i]=min_{i^\prime\ge i}A_s[i'],\)
\(B'_t[j]=min_{j^\prime\ge j}B_t[j'].\) We compute the Monotone Min-Plus Convolution \(A'_s*B'_t\) using the reduction provided by Lemma 5.6. \((A'_s*B'_t)[k^*]=A_s[i']+B_t[j'].\)
