## Running Time.

Initially, we call Lemma 5.3 to reduce from one given instance to \(O(n^\epsilon)\) listing instances, each provided with a low-doubling container. Lemma 5.3 runs in time \(O(n^{2-\delta})\) for some constant \(\delta=\delta(\rho,\epsilon)>0\). For each instance we call the algorithm implied by Hypothesis 1.7 on the container set \(\phi(H)\). This set has size \(N=O(n^{2-2\rho})\) and doubling \(K=O(n^\epsilon)\), and so this takes time \(O(n^{2-2\rho+O(\epsilon)})\). We then apply Lemma 5.9 in time<tbc>

\(|Y-\phi(H)||S|(logu)^{O(1)}=NK^{2c+2}(logu)^{O(1)}=n^{2-2\rho+O(\epsilon)}(logu)^{O(1)}.\)

<tbc>Then we reduce each listing instance (with threshold \(t=O(n^{2\rho})\)) further to \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2\rho})\) plain Min Plus Convolution subinstances by Lemma 2.14. This leaves us with \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2\rho+\epsilon})\) instances that the main part of the algorithm treats. For each pair of shifts \(s,t\in S\) we construct the sequences _A<sub>s</sub>,B<sub>t</sub>_ and \(A'_s,B'_t\) in linear time. Assuming the premise of Lemma 5.8, by Lemma 5.6 we can compute their convolution in time \(O(n^{2-\epsilon_0})\) for some \(\epsilon_0>0\). The total time is

\(\big(n^{2-\delta}+n^{2-2\rho+O(\epsilon)}+n^{2\rho+\epsilon+2-\epsilon_0}\big)(logu)^{O(1)}.\)

This becomes subquadratic for, say, \(\rho=\epsilon_0/8\) and by choosing \(0<\epsilon\le\epsilon_0/2\) sufficiently small so that the \(O(\epsilon)\) term becomes at most \(\rho\).

## 6 Lower Bounds for Intermediate Convolution Problems

In this section, we show our lower bounds for intermediate problems under the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis (also under the standard Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis if we assume Hypothesis 1.7).

We start with a useful lemma, which separately handles those heavy input entries.

**Lemma 6.1.** _Let_ (_A,B_) _be a given Min-Plus Convolution Listing instance with listing threshold_ \(n^\ell\) _for some_ \(\ell\ge 1/2\)_. Suppose C=A∗B is also given and let_ \(\delta>0\) _be a given constant. Then in_ \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2-\delta/2})\) _time, we can reduce it to a Min-Plus Convolution Listing instance_ \((A,B')\)_, where all entries in B that appear more than_ \(n^{\ell+\delta}\) _times are replaced with_ \(\perp\).

**Proof.** Call a value _v_ in _B_ heavy if it appears more than \(n^{\ell+\delta}\) times in _B_. Note that there could be at most \(O(n^{1-\ell-\delta})\) heavy value _v_. It suffices to list up to \(n^\ell\) witnesses (_i,j_) per output _C_\[_k_\], among those witnesses where _B_\[_j_\] is a heavy element.

To do so, let _v_ be an arbitrary heavy element in _B_, and define \(J_v=\{j\in[0,n]:B[j]=v\}\). For every distinct value _u_ in _A_, define \(I_u=\{i\in[0,n]:A[i]=u\}\) and \(K_{u+v}=\{k\in[0,2n]:C[k]=u+v\}\). These sets can be precomputed in near-linear time. Clearly, a pair \((i,j)\in I_u\times J_v\) is a witness for _C_\[_i+j_\] if \(i+j\in K_{u+v}\).

For a fixed pair of _u,v_, using FFT, we can verify whether each \(k\in K_{u+v}\) has a witness from \(I_u\times J_v\) in \(\widetilde{O}(n)\) total time for all _k_. Moreover, using standard sampling-based approaches (Lemma 2.15), we can list up to \(\lfloor\frac{|I_u|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\rfloor\) witnesses per \(k\in K_{u+v}\) in \(\widetilde{O}(\lfloor\frac{|I_u|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\rfloor n+1)\) time. The +1 term in the previous running time is needed for the case \(\lfloor\frac{|I_u|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\rfloor=0\). Over all values of _v_ and _u_, the total cost for this case is thus (up to polylog(_n_) factor)

\(\sum_u\sum_v\left(\left\lfloor\frac{|I_u|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\right\rfloor n+1\right)\le n^{1-\ell-\delta}\sum_u\left(\frac{|I_u|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\cdot n+1\right)\le O(n^{2-\delta/2}).\)

Hence, it suffices to consider some \(k\in K_{u+v}\) for sub-instances (_I<sub>u</sub>,J<sub>v</sub>,K_<sub>_u+v_</sub>) where _k_ has at least \(\lfloor\frac{|I_u|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\rfloor\) witnesses (and we have not found up to \(n^\ell\) witnesses in the input instance (_A,B_) for _k_). In this case, we simply spend _O_(|_I<sub>u</sub>_|) time to list all the witnesses for _k_ in (_I<sub>u</sub>,J<sub>v</sub>,K_<sub>_u+v_</sub>). Let _U<sub>k</sub>_ be the set of _u_ where we need to perform this brute-force over _I<sub>u</sub>_ for _k_. Note that for a fixed _k_, _C_\[_k_\]=_u+v_ is fixed; in addition, the number of heavy values _v_ is \(O(n^{1-\ell-\delta})\), so the number of _u_ where \(k\in K_{u+v}\) is also \(O(n^{1-\ell-\delta})\). Hence \(|U_k|\le O(n^{1-\ell-\delta})\).

As we only need to output \(n^\ell\) total witnesses for _k_, we have<tbc>

\(\sum_{u\in U_k}\left\lfloor\frac{|I_u|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\right\rfloor\le n^\ell,\)

<tbc>which implies (recall we assume \(\ell\ge 1/2\))<tbc>

\(\sum_{u\in U_k}\frac{|I_u|}{n^{1-\ell-\delta/2}}\le|U_k|+n^\ell\le n^{1-\ell-\delta}+n^\ell=O(n^\ell).\)

<tbc>Hence, the cost for a particular value of _k_ is

\(O\left(\sum_{u\in U_k}|I_u|\right)\le O(n^\ell\cdot n^{1-\ell-\delta/2})=O(n^{1-\delta/2}).\)

Summing over all possible _k_ gives an \(O(n^{2-\delta/2})\) running time, as desired.

## 6.1 Min-Max Convolution

**Theorem 1.9** (Min-Max Convolution)**.** _Min-Max Convolution cannot be solved in time_ \(O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})\) _(for any constant_ \(\epsilon>0\)_), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails._

**Proof.** Suppose Min-Max Convolution can be solved in \(O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})\) time for some \(\epsilon>0\) by an algorithm A. In order to show this contradicts the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis, by Corollary 5.2 with \(\gamma=\frac{1}{2}\), it suffices to give a truly sub-quadratic time algorithm for Min-Plus Convolution instances (_A,B_) where the elements are from \([\sqrt{n}]\) while we need to list up to \(\sqrt{n}\) witnesses per output.

Because the universe is \([\sqrt{n}]\), _C=A∗B_ can be computed in \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})\) time. By Lemma 6.1, we can further assume every non-\(\perp\) value in _B_ appears at most \(n^{1/2+\epsilon/3}\) times.

For every \(b\in[\sqrt{n}]\), we define a Min-Max Convolution instance (_A<sub>b</sub>,B<sub>b</sub>_), where _A<sub>b</sub>_\[_i_\]=_A_\[_i_\] for every \(i\in[0,n]\), and \(B_b[j]=-\infty\) if _B_\[_j_\]=_b_ and \(B_b[j]=\infty\) otherwise. Let _C<sub>b</sub>_=Min-Max(_A<sub>b</sub>,B<sub>b</sub>_). It is not difficult to see that, (_i,j_) is a witness for _C_\[_k_\] (i.e., _A_\[_i_\]+_B_\[_j_\]=_C_\[_k_\] and _i+j=k_), if and only if for some _b_, _C<sub>b</sub>_\[_k_\]=_C_\[_k_\]-_b_ and (_i,j_) is a witness for _C<sub>b</sub>_\[_k_\] in the Min-Max Convolution instance defined for _b_.

Consider the following algorithm. We enumerate \(b\in[\sqrt{n}]\), create _A<sub>b</sub>_ and _B<sub>b</sub>_, and compute _C<sub>b</sub>_=Min-Max(_A<sub>b</sub>,B<sub>b</sub>_) using A in \(O(n^{1.5-\epsilon})\) time per _b_. By standard sampling-based approaches (Lemma 2.14), we can further list \(n^{2\epsilon/3}\) witnesses for every _C<sub>b</sub>_\[_k_\] in \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5-\epsilon/3})\) time using A as a black-box. This step takes \(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n}\cdot n^{1.5-\epsilon/3})=\widetilde{O}(n^{2-\epsilon/3})\) time over all \(b\in[\sqrt{n}]\).

What remains to consider are those _C<sub>b</sub>_\[_k_\] that have more than \(n^{2\epsilon/3}\) witnesses and _C<sub>b</sub>_\[_k_\]=_C_\[_k_\]-_b_. We call such a pair (_b,k_) heavy. For a heavy pair, we enumerate all elements in \(S_b:=\{j\in[n]:B[j]=b\}\) (this can be done in _O_(|_S<sub>b</sub>_|) time by computing these sets in preprocessing), and check whether each \(j\in S_b\) forms a witness for _C<sub>b</sub>_\[_k_\]. Recall each value in _B_ appears at most \(n^{1/2+\epsilon/3}\) time, so the cost for each heavy pair is \(O(n^{1/2+\epsilon/3})\). Since we only need to list up to _n_<sup>1/2</sup> witness per _C_\[_k_\], we only need to resolve \(n^{1/2-2\epsilon/3}\) heavy pairs for a particular value of _k_ before we find enough witnesses for _C_\[_k_\]. Hence, we only need to handle \(O(n^{3/2-2\epsilon/3})\) heavy pairs in total, and thus the overall running time for this case is \(O(n^{2-\epsilon/3})\).

## 6.2 Min-Equality Convolution

**Theorem 1.10** (Min-Equality Convolution)**.** _Min-Equality Convolution cannot be solved in time_ \(O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})\) _(for any constant_ \(\epsilon>0\)_), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails._

**Proof.** Suppose Min-Equality Convolution can be solved in \(O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})\) time for some \(\epsilon>0\) by an algorithm A. Similar as before, it suffices to give a truly sub-quadratic time algorithm for Min-Plus Convolution Listing instances (_A,B_) where the elements are from \([\sqrt{n}]\) while we need to list up to \(\sqrt{n}\) witnesses per output.

We can compute _C=A∗B_ in \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})\) time and we can further assume every non-\(\perp\) value in _B_ appears at most \(n^{1/2+\epsilon/3}\) time by Lemma 6.1.

For every \(\Delta\in\{-\sqrt{n},\dots,\sqrt{n}\}\), we define a Min-Equality Convolution instance \((A_\Delta,B_\Delta)\), where \(A_\Delta[i]=A[i]+\Delta\) for every \(i\in[0,n]\) and \(B_\Delta=B\). Intuitively, we aim to use \(\Delta\) to represent _B_\[_j_\]-_A_\[_i_\]. Let \(C_\Delta=\text{Min-Equal}(A_\Delta,B_\Delta)\). The following claim shows how the witnesses in the Min-Equality Convolution instance \((A_\Delta,B_\Delta)\) are related to the witnesses in the Min-Plus Convolution instance (_A,B_).

**Claim 6.2.** _Let_ \((i_0,j_0,k_0)\in[0,n]^3\) _be a triple with i_0+_j_0=_k_0_, and let_ \(\Delta=B[j_0]-A[i_0]\)_. Then, A_\[_i_0\]+_B_\[_j_0\]=_C_\[_k_0\] _holds if and only if both_ \(2C_\Delta[k_0]=C[k_0]+\Delta\) _and_ \(A_\Delta[i_0]=B_\Delta[j_0]=C_\Delta[k_0]\) _hold._ **Proof.** We first show the forward direction. By definition, \(2C_\Delta[k_0]=2min_{i+j=k_0A_\Delta[i]=B_\Delta[j]}B_\Delta[j]=min_{i+j=k_0A[i]+\Delta=B[j]}\{A[i]+\Delta+B[j]\}\)
\(\ge min_{i+j=k_0}\{A[i]+\Delta+B[j]\}=C[k_0]+\Delta.\) Additionally, since \(A_\Delta[i_0]=A[i_0]+\Delta=B[j_0]=B_\Delta[j_0]\), \(2C_\Delta[k_0]\le 2B_\Delta[j_0]=A[i_0]+\Delta+B[j_0]=C[k_0]+\Delta.\) Hence, we have \(2C_\Delta[k_0]=C[k_0]+\Delta\). Moreover, we have \(C_\Delta[k_0]=B_\Delta[j_0]\) since the above inequality is tight, so \(A_\Delta[i_0]=B_\Delta[j_0]=C_\Delta[k_0]\) holds as claimed. Now we consider the reverse direction. ## 6.4 Min-Witness Convolution

The following lemma is the key step in the reduction to Min-Witness Convolution.

**Lemma 6.4.** _Suppose Min-Witness Convolution can be solved in O(T(n_)) _time, and let_ \(1/3\le\ell\le 1\) _be a constant. Then in_ \(\widetilde{O}(T(n)\cdot n^\ell)\) _time we can list up to_ \(n^\ell\) _witnesses for each output in Min-Plus Convolution instances_ (_A,B_) _where the universe of all elements in A has size n_<sup>1/3</sup>_, and the universe of all elements in B is_ \(\{0,\perp\}\)_. The algorithm succeeds with high probability._

**Proof.** First, since \(B[j]\in\{0,\perp\}\), we can replace each element in _A_ by its rank in the universe without loss of generality, and hence assume that the universe of elements in _A_ is \[_n_<sup>1/3</sup>\]. Let _C=A∗B_, which can be computed in \(\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3})\) time.

By trying all sampling rates _p_=1,2<sup>-1</sup>,2<sup>-2</sup>_,..._, and only keeping sampled elements in _B_ as their original values while setting all other elements as \(\perp\), then with high probability, there will be a round where the number of witnesses for _C_\[_k_\] is \(\Theta(n^\ell)\) if the number of witnesses for _C_\[_k_\] in the original instance is more than \(n^\ell\). Hence, we only need to handle _C_\[_k_\] with \(O(n^\ell)\) witnesses.

In addition, it suffices to list _n_<sup>1/3</sup> witnesses per _C_\[_k_\] in \(\widetilde{O}(T(n)n^{1/3})\) time: If \(\ell>1/3\), we can randomly partition _B_ to \(\Theta(n^{\ell-1/3})\) random subsequences (by keeping elements not in the corresponding subsequence as \(\perp\)), so that for every _C_\[_k_\], each subsequence contains at most _n_<sup>1/3</sup> witnesses, with high probability.

Before we give the actual reduction, let us first give some intuition. The difficulty of reducing Min-Plus Convolution to Min-Witness Convolution is that, in Min-Witness Convolution, there is no value in the inputs. Hence, we somehow need to encode the weight information in the indices. One potential way is to take monotone subsequences of _A_, and create Boolean sequence \(A'\) where \(A'[i]=1\) if _i_ is in the chosen subsequence and create Boolean sequence \(B'\) where \(B'[i]=1\) if _B_\[_i_\]=0. Because the chosen subsequence is monotone, the Min-Witness Convolution naturally favors candidates (_i,k-i_) where _A_\[_i_\] is smaller, as intended. One potential way to choose monotone subsequences is the following: We take all the 1’s in the first _n_<sup>2/3</sup> entries of _A_, all the 2’s in the second _n_<sup>2/3</sup> entries of _A_, and so on. The downside is that, some _C_\[_k_\] might have many witnesses from the subsequence, while some have few. To overcome this issue, we randomly shuffle the indices and work over the shuffled sequences.

Let _N_ be a prime number from \[2_n,_4_n_\], which can be found deterministically in \(\widetilde{O}(n)\) time. We extend _A_ and _B_ to length _N_, where the extra elements are \(\perp\). Now Min-Plus Convolution _C_ between _A_ and _B_ can be equivalently defined by \(C[k]=min_{i\in\mathbb{F}_N}\{A[i]+B[k-i]\}\).

We will repeat the following \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1/3})\) times. Let _x_∼F_<sub>N</sub>_\\{0} and _y_∼F_<sub>N</sub>_ be uniformly random, and let \(f_{x,y}:\mathbb{F}_N\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_N\) where \(f_{x,y}(i)=i\cdot x+y\). Now define the shuffled sequences _A<sub>x,y</sub>_ and _B<sub>x,y</sub>_, where

\(A_{x,y}[f_{x,y}(i)]=A[i]\text{and}B_{x,y}[f_{x,y}(i)]=B[i]\text{for}i\in\mathbb{F}_N.\)

_A<sub>x,y</sub>_ and _B<sub>x,y</sub>_ are well-defined because _f<sub>x,y</sub>_ is invertible. Consider two subsets \(S_{x,y}=\{i\in\mathbb{F}_N:A_{x,y}[i]=\lfloor i/N^{2/3}\rfloor\}\) and \(T_{x,y}=\{i\in\mathbb{F}_N:B_{x,y}[i]=0\}\). We then create two Boolean sequences \(A'_{x,y}\) and \(B'_{x,y}\), which are the indicator sequences for _S<sub>x,y</sub>_ and _T<sub>x,y</sub>_ respectively.

The following claim shows why it is useful to compute the Min-Witness Convolution between \(A'_{x,y}\) and \(B'_{x,y}\) (even though the indices of them are from F_<sub>N</sub>_ rather than Z, we can still use standard Min-Witness Convolution with some simple postprocessing to compute it).

Then the probability that i_0 _is the unique element in Ik that satisfies_ \(f_{x,y}(i)\in S_{x,y}\) _is_ \(\Omega(1/N^{1/3})\). **Proof.** Note that every \(i\in I_k\) has the same value _A_\[_i_\]. **Theorem 1.12** (Min-Witness Convolution)**.** _Min-Witness Convolution cannot be solved in time_ \(O(n^{4/3-\epsilon})\) _(for any constant_ \(\epsilon>0\)_), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails._

**Proof.** Suppose Min-Witness Convolution can be solved in \(O(n^{4/3-\epsilon})\) time for some \(\epsilon>0\) by an algorithm A. In order to show this contradicts the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis, by Corollary 5.2 with \(\gamma=\frac{2}{3}\), it suffices to give a truly sub-quadratic time algorithm for \(\text{MPConvList}(n,n^{2/3}|u\le n^{1/3})\). For every \(b\in[n^{1/3}]\), we solve a sub-instance between (_A,B<sub>b</sub>_), where _B<sub>b</sub>_\[_j_\]=0 if _B_\[_j_\]=_b_, and \(B_b[j]=\infty\) otherwise. If _C<sub>b</sub>_\[_k_\]=_C_\[_k_\]-_b_, and Lemma 6.4 lists fewer than \(n^{1/3+2\epsilon/3}\) witnesses for _C<sub>b</sub>_\[_k_\], then we have listed all witnesses (_i,j_) satisfying _B_\[_j_\]=_b_ for _C_\[_k_\]. ## 7 Asymmetric BSG Theorem

In this section, we show an algorithmic version of the Asymmetric BSG Theorem (originally proved by Tao and Vu \[TV06, Section 2.6\]), stated as follows.

**Theorem 2.4** (Asymmetric BSG Theorem)**.** _Let_ \(\epsilon>0\) _and_ \(0<\alpha\le 1\)_. Let_ \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _be sets with energy_ \(E(A,B)\ge\alpha|A|^2|B|\)_. Then there are sets_ \(H,\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _and some_ \(K\le O_\epsilon(\alpha^{-O_\epsilon(1)}(1+|B|/|A|)^\epsilon)\) _such that:_

• \(|H+H|\le K|H|\),<tbc>

• \(|H||\Lambda|\le K|B|\),<tbc>

• \(|A\cap H|\ge|A|/K\) _and_ \(|B\cap(H+\Lambda)|\ge|B|/K\).

_Moreover, there is a randomized algorithm to compute_ \(H,\Lambda\) _in time_ \(\widetilde{O}((|A|+|B|)K)\).

### 7.1 Preliminary Lemmas

Our algorithmic proof of Theorem 2.4 is heavily based on the original proof for the non-algorithmic version by Tao and Vu \[TV06, Section 2.6\]. We turn each step into an efficient algorithm using mostly basic ideas.

We start with the following definition from \[TV06, Definition 2.32\]:

**Definition 7.1** (Symmetry Sets)**.** For \(A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) and \(0<\alpha\le 1\), we define the _symmetry set_<tbc>

\(\text{Sym}(A;\alpha)=\{x\in A-A:r_{A-A}(x)\ge\alpha|A|\}.\)

Note that \(0\in\mathrm{Sym}(A;\alpha)\) and \(\mathrm{Sym}(A;\alpha)=-\mathrm{Sym}(A;\alpha)\). Moreover, it holds that \(|\mathrm{Sym}(A;\alpha)|\le\frac{|A|}{\alpha},\) which follows readily from \(\sum_{x\in A-A}r_{A-A}(x)=|A|^2\). In the notation from before one can equivalently express the symmetry set as a set of popular differences, \(\mathrm{Sym}(A;\alpha)=\mathrm{Pop}(A,-A;\alpha|A|)\). We need the following lemma corresponding to \[TV06, Lemma 2.34\]. **Lemma 7.2** (Dyadic Pigeonhole Principle)**.** _Let_ \(0<\alpha<1\) _and let_ \(A,D\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\) _be such that_ \(\sum_{x\in D}r_{A-A}(x)\ge\alpha|A|^2.\) _Then there is a subset_ \(D'\subseteq D\) _such that, for every_ \(x\in D'\), \(r_{A-A}(x)\ge\Omega\left(\frac{\alpha}{1+\mathrm{log}\frac{1}{\alpha}+\mathrm{log}(1+\frac{|D|}{|A|})}\cdot\frac{|A|^2}{|D'|}\right).\) _Moreover, there is a randomized algorithm that, given A,_ \(\alpha\) _and D, computes such a set_ \(D'\) _in time_ \(\widetilde{O}(|A|+|D|/\alpha)\). **Proof.** We first call Lemma 2.5 on the sets _A,-A,D_ with parameter \(\epsilon=\mathrm{min}(\frac{\alpha|A|}{8|D|},1)\) to approximate the multiplicities _r__A-A_(_x_) for all \(x\in D\) by \(0\le\tilde{r}(x)\le|A|\) within additive error \(|r_{A-A}(x)-\tilde{r}(x)|\le\epsilon|A|=\frac{\alpha|A|^2}{8|D|}.\) Let \(D^*=\left\{x\in D:\tilde{r}(x)\ge\frac{\alpha|A|^2}{4|D|}\right\}.\) This set is chosen so that for all \(x\in D^*\) we have \(r_{A-A}(x)\ge\tilde{r}(x)/2\). Further observe that \(\sum_{x\in D^*}\tilde{r}(x)\ge\sum_{x\in D}\tilde{r}(x)-\sum_{x\in D\backslash D^*}\tilde{r}(x)\)
\(\ge\sum_{x\in D}\tilde{r}(x)-|D|\cdot\frac{\alpha|A|^2}{4|D|}\)
\(\ge\sum_{x\in D}r_{A-A}(x)-|D|\cdot\frac{\alpha|A|^2}{8|D|}-|D|\cdot\frac{\alpha|A|^2}{4|D|}\)
\(\ge\frac{\alpha|A|^2}{2}.\) Now let _L_ be the smallest integer with \(2^{-L}<\frac{\alpha|A|}{2|D|}\), and consider the partition of _D_∗ into _D_1_,...,DL_ defined by \(D_\ell=\left\{x\in D^*:\frac{|A|}{2^\ell}<\tilde{r}(x)\le\frac{|A|}{2^{\ell-1}}\right\}.\)

By the pigeonhole principle at least one part \(1\le\ell\le L\) satisfies \(\sum_{x\in D_\ell}\tilde{r}(x)\ge\frac{\alpha|A|^2}{2L};\) take that part and report \(D'=D_\ell\). Indeed, each \(x\in D_\ell\) satisfies \(r_{A-A}(x)\ge\frac{\tilde{r}(x)}{2}\ge\frac{|A|}{2^{\ell+1}}\ge\frac{\sum_{x\in D_\ell}\tilde{r}(x)}{4|D_\ell|}\ge\frac{\alpha|A|^2}{8L|D_\ell|},\) which is as claimed, recalling that \(L\le 1+log\frac{1}{\alpha}+log(1+\frac{|D|}{|A|})\). Finally, consider the running time. Lemma 2.5 takes time \(\widetilde{O}(|A|/\epsilon+|D|)=\widetilde{O}(|A|+|D|/\alpha)\). All subsequent steps, including the construction of _D_∗, its partitioning, and selecting the relevant part \(D_\ell\), run in linear time _O_(|_D_|). We also rely on the following lemma, which is a combination of \[TV06, Lemma 2.33\] and \[TV06, Lemma 2.34\]. **Lemma 7.3.** _Let_ \(0<\alpha\le 1\) _and let A,S be sets with_ \(S\subseteq Sym(A;\alpha)\)_. Then:_ \(|\{(s_1,s_2)\in S^2:s_1-s_2\in Sym(A;\alpha^2/2)\}|\ge\frac{\alpha^2|S|^2}{2}.\) **Proof.** Supposing otherwise, \(E(A,S)=\sum_{s_1,s_2\in S}r_{A-A}(s_1-s_2)\)
\(<\frac{\alpha^2|S|^2}{2}\cdot|A|+|S|^2\cdot\frac{\alpha^2|A|}{2}\)
\(=\alpha^2|S|^2|A|.\) But at the same time, by Cauchy-Schwarz, \(E(A,S)\ge\sum_{a\in A}r_{A+S}(a)^2\)
\(\ge\frac{\left(\sum_{a\in A}r_{A+S}(a)\right)^2}{|A|}\)
\(=\frac{\left(\sum_{s\in S}r_{A-A}(s)\right)^2}{|A|}\)
\(\ge\frac{(|S|\cdot\alpha|A|)^2}{|A|}\)
\(=\alpha^2|S|^2|A|,\) which shows the desired contradiction.

## 7.2 Existential Proof In this subsection we finally prove the existential statement of Theorem 2.4. Recall that we start from integer sets _A,B_ with energy \(E(A,B)\ge\alpha|A|^2|B|.\) The proof can conceptually be split into four steps. In the first step we will successively replace _A_ by "smoother" sets _A_1_,A_2_,..._ that admit more additive structure. As an instructive example, consider the set _B_={1_,...,|B_|} and let _A_ be a random subset of _B_. When _B_ is large compared to _A_, _A_ essentially admits no additive structure at all. We will therefore replace _A_ by smoother sets (think of _A-A,_2_A_-2_A,..._) converging to the highly structured set _B_. Once we reach a set that is sufficiently structured, in the second step we apply the symmetric BSG theorem to identify a large low-doubling subset _H_. In the third step we unroll the iterative smoothing procedure to relate _H_ to the initial set _A_. In the fourth step we relate _H_ to _B_. Following \[TV06\], we introduce a useful piece of notation. We write _f=Oj(g_) if there exists a positive constant _C(j_) (that only depends on _j_) such that \(f\le C(j)\cdot\alpha^{-C(j)}\cdot\left(1+log\frac{|B|}{|A|}\right)^{C(j)}\cdot g;\) that is, the _Oj_ notation hides constant factors, polynomial factors in \(1/\alpha\), and polylogarithmic factors in |_B|/|A_|. Similarly define \(f=\Omega_j(g)\). ### Step 1: Iteratively Smoothing _A_. Let \(J=J(\epsilon)\) be a constant to be fixed later. Let \(\alpha_1=\alpha/2\) and recursively define \(\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_J\) by \(\alpha_{j+1}=\alpha_j^2/2\). Note that \(\alpha_1>\cdots>\alpha_J>0\) and \(\alpha_j=\Omega_j(1)\). We will inductively construct a sequence of sets _A_0_,A_1_,...,AJ_ with the following properties: (i) for all \(1\le j\le J\), \(A_j\subseteq Sym(B;\alpha_j)\), (ii) for all \(0\le j (iii) for all \(0\le j\le J\), \(|A_j|=\Omega_j(|A|)\). In fact, Property (iii) is always implied by Property (ii): If \(\sum_{x\in A_{j+1}}r_{A_j-A_j}(x)\ge\Omega_j(|A_j|^2)\), then we must have \(|A_{j+1}|\ge\Omega_j(|A_j|)\), and then Property (iii) follows by induction. For this reason we will only ensure Properties (i) and (ii) in the following construction. The base case is concerned with the construction of _A_0 and _A_1. We trivially take _A_0=_A_. To construct _A_1, first observe that \(E(A,B)=\sum_{a_1,a_2\in A}r_{B-B}(a_1-a_2)\)
\(\le\sum_{a_1,a_2\in A}\frac{\alpha|B|}{2}+|\{(a_1,a_2)\in A^2:a_1-a_2\in Sym(B;\alpha/2)\}|\cdot|B|.\) In particular, recalling that \(E(A,B)\ge\alpha|A|^2|B|\), and letting \(D=Sym(B;\alpha/2)\), we must have \(\sum_{x\in D}r_{A-A}(x)\ge\frac{\alpha|A|^2}{2}.\)

Hence, Lemma 7.2 yields a set \(A_1\subseteq D=Sym(B;\alpha/2)\) that directly satisfies both Properties (i) and (ii). Now focus on the inductive case, i.e., let \(j\ge 1\), assume that _Aj_ has already been constructed, and focus on the construction of _A__j_+1. By (i) we have \(A_j\subseteq Sym(B;\alpha_j)\). Apply Lemma 7.3 with \(\alpha_j\) and sets _B,Aj_, yielding that \(|\{(a_1,a_2)\in A_j^2:a_1-a_2\in Sym(B;\alpha_j^2/2)\}|\ge\frac{\alpha_j^2|A_j|^2}{2}.\) Next, apply Lemma 7.2 with parameter \(\alpha_{j+1}=\alpha_j^2/2\) on the sets \(A_j,Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})\) to construct a set \(A_{j+1}\subseteq Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})\) satisfying, for all \(x\in A_{j+1}\), \(r_{A_j-A_j}(x)=\Omega\left(\frac{\alpha_j}{1+log\frac{1}{\alpha_j}+log(1+\frac{|Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})|}{|A_j|})}\cdot\frac{|A_j|^2}{|A_{j+1}|}\right)=\Omega_j\left(\frac{|A_j|^2}{|A_{j+1}|}\right).\) In the last step we used that \(|A_j|=\Omega_j(|A|)\) (by (iii)) and \(|Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})|\le|B|/\alpha_{j+1}\); taken together these imply that \(log(1+|Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})|/|A_j|)\) can be hidden in the \(\Omega_j\) notation. Evidently, the set _A__j_+1 satisfies both Properties (i) and (ii), completing the construction. ## Step 2: Constructing _H_ by the BSG Theorem. Take \(0\le j_j_+1|/|_Aj_|. Recall that |_A_0|=|_A_| and that \(|A_J|\le|Sym(B;\alpha_J)|\le|B|/\alpha_J=O_J(|B|)\) by Property (i). Thus, writing _L_=1+|_B|/|A_|, we must have \(|A_{j+1}|=O_J\big(L^{1/J}\cdot|A_j|\big).\) Moreover, Property (ii) implies that \(E(A_j)=\sum_{x\in A_j-A_j}r_{A_j-A_j}(x)^2\)
\(\ge\sum_{x\in A_{j+1}}r_{A_j-A_j}(x)^2\)
\(=\Omega_j\big(\frac{|A_j|^4}{|A_{j+1}|}\big)\)
\(=\Omega_J\big(\frac{|A_j|^3}{L^{1/J}}\big).\) In this situation, the symmetric BSG theorem (Theorem 2.3) applies, yielding some _Kj=OJ(L__O_(1_/J_)) and a set _H_ with \(|H|\le K_j|A_j|,\) (10) and \(|H+H|\le K_j|H|,\) (11) and \(|A_j\cap H|\ge\frac{|A_j|}{K_j}.\) (12)

Equation (11) is claimed as in the theorem statement (once we fix the parameter _J_). Equations (10) and (12) involve _A<sub>j</sub>_ rather than _A_; in the following we show that these imply similar statements for _A_.

## Step 3: Relating _H_ to _A_.

To relate _H_ to _A_, we traverse the sets _A=A_<sub>0</sub>_,A_<sub>1</sub>_,...,A<sub>j</sub> backwards_. More precisely, we deduce from \(|A_j\cap(H+x_j)|\ge|A_j|/K_j\) that \(|A_{j-1}\cap(H+x_{j-1})|\ge|A_{j-1}|/K_{j-1}\), for some shifts _x_<sub>_j_-1</sub> and parameters _K_<sub>_j_-1</sub> (we have _x<sub>j</sub>_=0). Indeed, assuming \(|A_j\cap(H+x_j)|\ge|A_j|/K_j\), Property (ii) implies that<tbc>

\(|\{(a_1,a_2)\in A_{j-1}^2:a_1-a_2\in(H+x_j)\}|\ge\Omega_j\big(\frac{|A_{j-1}|^2}{K_j}\big),\)

<tbc>or equivalently,<tbc>

\(\sum_{a\in A_{j-1}}|A_{j-1}\cap(H+x_j+a)|\ge\Omega_j\big(\frac{|A_{j-1}|^2}{K_j}\big).\)

<tbc>In particular, there is some _a_ such that \(|A_{j-1}\cap(H+x_j+a)|\ge\Omega_j(|A_{j-1}|/K_j)\). Choosing _x_<sub>_j_-1</sub>=_x<sub>j</sub>+a_ and _K_<sub>_j_-1</sub>=_O<sub>j</sub>(K<sub>j</sub>_), the claim follows. By induction we learn that

\(|A\cap(H+x_0)|\ge\frac{|A|}{K_0},\) (13)

for some translate _x_<sub>0</sub> and some parameter

\(K_0=O_j(K_j)=O_J(L^{O(1/J)}).\)

Equation (13) is exactly as claimed in the theorem statement, when shifting _H_ by _x_<sub>0</sub>.

## Step 4: Relating _H_ to _B_.

We finally relate _H_ to _B_. Combining Property (i) with Equations (10) and (12) implies that<tbc>

\(|H\cap\mathrm{Sym}(B;\alpha_j)|\ge\frac{|H|}{K_j^2}.\)

<tbc>In particular, by definition of \(\mathrm{Sym}(B;\alpha_j)\) we have<tbc>

\(|\{(b,h)\in B\times H:b+h\in B\}|\ge\frac{\alpha_j}{K_j^2}\cdot|B||H|.\) (14)

<tbc>Let \(\Lambda\subseteq B\) be a random subset, sampled with rate \(p=\mathrm{min}(1,4K_j^2/(\alpha_j|H|))\). Then, with constant probability,

\(|B\cap(H+\Lambda)|\ge\frac{\alpha_j}{4K_j^2}\cdot|B|.\) (15)

To see this, call an element \(b\in B\) _relevant_ if<tbc>

\(r_{B+H}(b)\ge\frac{\alpha_j}{2K_j^2}\cdot|H|.\)

Equation (14) entails that there must be at least \(\alpha_j/2K_j^2\cdot|B|\) relevant elements. But each relevant item is not covered in \(H+\Lambda\) with probability at most \((1-p)^{\frac{\alpha_j}{2K_j^2\cdot|H|}}\) . When _p_=1, this trivially equals 0; otherwise,<tbc>

\((1-p)^{\frac{\alpha_j}{2K_j^2\cdot|H|}}\le exp(-p\cdot\frac{\alpha_j}{2K_j^2}\cdot|H|)\le exp(-2)<\frac{1}{4}.\)

<tbc>By Markov’s inequality, with probability at least 1/2, at least half the relevant elements are covered by \(H+\Lambda\). This proves Equation (15). At the same time, \(\Lambda\) satisfies the following size bound with high probability:

\(|\Lambda|\le O\left(\frac{K_j^2}{\alpha_j}\cdot\frac{|B|}{|H|}\right).\) (16)

### Wrapping Up.

All in all, Equations (11), (13), (15) and (16) are as claimed in Theorem 2.4; it only remains to choose appropriate parameters. All these equations have an overhead of the form _O<sub>J</sub>(L_<sup>_O_(1_/J_)</sup>), i.e.,<tbc>

\(C(J)\cdot\alpha^{-C(J)}\cdot L^{C_0/J}\cdot(logL)^{C(J)},\)

<tbc>for some absolute constant _C_<sub>0</sub> and some constant _C(J_) depending on _J_. Choosing \(J>C_0/\epsilon\), this overhead indeed takes the form

\(K=O_\epsilon(\alpha^{-O_\epsilon(1)}L^\epsilon).\)

The proof of Theorem 2.4 is complete.

## 7.3 Efficient Algorithm

In this section we finally argue that the previous proof can be implemented by an efficient algorithm, running in time \(\widetilde{O}((|A|+|B|)K)\) for some \(K\le O_\epsilon(\alpha^{-O_\epsilon(1)}L^\epsilon)\). To this end, we revisit the four steps from before and comment on their implementations.

### Step 1: Iteratively Smoothing _A_.

In the first step we explicitly compute the sets _A_<sub>1</sub>_,...,A<sub>J</sub>_. This step is already almost completely algorithmic. Each set _A_<sub>_j_+1</sub> is constructed by one call to Lemma 7.2 on input _A<sub>j</sub>_ and \(D=Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})\); the only problem is that we do not have access to \(Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})\). Instead, we will compute some superset<tbc>

\(Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1})\subseteq D\subseteq Sym(B;\alpha_{j+1}/2)\)

<tbc>by Lemma 3.3 in time \(\widetilde{O}(|B|/\alpha_{j+1})\). This leaves the correctness unchanged. The running time of Lemma 7.2 can then be bounded by

\(\widetilde{O}\left(|A_j|+\frac{|D|}{\alpha_{j+1}}\right)=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{|B|}{\alpha_{j+1}^2}\right).\)

The total time of step 1 is dominated by the final iteration, \(\widetilde{O}(|B|/\alpha_J^2)\), which is within the budget.<tbc>

### Step 2: Constructing **_H_** by the BSG Theorem.

In step 2 we first identify the index _j_ minimizing |_A_<sub>_j_+1</sub>|/|_A<sub>j</sub>_|. Since we have computed the sets _A_<sub>1</sub>_,...,A<sub>J</sub>_ explicitly, this can be done in linear time. Then we apply the BSG theorem (Theorem 2.3) to the set _A<sub>j</sub>_ to construct _H_. This runs in time \(\widetilde{O}(|A_j|K_j)\), for some _K<sub>j</sub>=O<sub>J</sub>(L_<sup>_O_(1_/J_)</sup>) as before. Again, recalling that \(|A_j|\le|B|/\alpha_j\) by Property (iii), this is within the claimed time budget.

### Step 3: Relating **_H_** to **_A_**.

The only data that we need to compute in this step is the shift _x_<sub>0</sub> satisfying Equation (13), i.e.,<tbc>

\(|A\cap(H+x_0)|\ge\frac{|A|}{K_0}.\)

<tbc>In fact, we settle for a slightly weaker condition. Namely, observe that this shift _x_<sub>0</sub> is equivalently an element of Pop(_A,-H_;|_A|/K_<sub>0</sub>). Hence, to find _x_<sub>0</sub> we may run Lemma 3.3 to compute a set sandwiched between Pop(_A,-H_;|_A|/K_<sub>0</sub>) and Pop(_A,-H_;|_A|/_2_K_<sub>0</sub>), and pick any element _x_<sub>0</sub> from that set. By definition, that element satisfies

\(|A\cap(H+x_0)|\ge\frac{|A|}{2K_0}.\)

We may increase _K_<sub>0</sub> to 2_K_<sub>0</sub> without any harm, and then _x_<sub>0</sub> is as claimed in Equation (13).

The running time is dominated by the call to Lemma 3.3 in time \(\widetilde{O}(|H|K_0)\). By Equation (10) and Property (iii) this is at most \(\widetilde{O}(|A_j|K_jK_0)=\widetilde{O}(|B|K_jK_0/\alpha_j)\), which is within the budget.

### Step 4: Relating **_H_** to **_B_**.

The final step only involves the construction of \(\Lambda\). Recall that \(\Lambda\) is constructed as a random subset of _B_, sampled with an appropriate rate _p_. We have argued that with constant probability, the size \(|B\cap(H+\Lambda)|\) is at least as large as claimed in Equation (15). The only modification in our algorithm is to amplify the success probability. That is, we sample \(R=\Theta(log|B|)\) sets \(\Lambda_1,\dots,\Lambda_R\), compute the sumsets \(H+\Lambda_1,\dots,H+\Lambda_R\) by brute-force, and report the set \(\Lambda_r\) maximizing \(|B\cap(H+\Lambda_r)|\). With high probability that choice satisfies Equation (15). Moreover, with high probability all sets \(\Lambda_1,\dots,\Lambda_R\) simultaneously satisfy the size bound from Equation (16),<tbc>

\(|\Lambda_1|,\dots,|\Lambda_R|\le O\left(\frac{K_j^2}{\alpha_j}\cdot\frac{|B|}{|H|}\right).\)

<tbc>The running time of step 4 is therefore bounded by

\(O\left(\sum_{r=1}^R(|B|+|H||\Lambda_r|)\right)=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{K_j^2}{\alpha_j}\cdot|B|\right).\)

This is within the claimed time budget.
